articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
US stock futures diverged in premarket trading on Thursday as Alphabet's Q3 earnings sparked a sell-off in the stock and AI jitters returned to markets, dragging on the tech-heavy indexes.
Futures on the Dow Jones Industrial Average ( YM=F ) fell below the flatline. Those on the S&P 500 ( ES=F ) slid 0.2%, while contracts for the Nasdaq-100 ( NQ=F ) fell 1%.
Tech stocks snapped a positive run this week as investors digested the Fed's rate pause on Wednesday and earnings from Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ). Microsoft beat analyst expectations on the top and bottom lines, while Alphabet sales came up short . Although Google posted cloud growth of 103%, concerns about its free cash flow and AI return on investment were the albatross on the company's quarter.
A sell-off in AI names spread to Asian markets as South Korea's Kospi ( ^KS11 ) index declined. The iShares Semiconductor Index ETF ( SOXX ) also skidded after hours as Nvidia ( NVDA ), AMD ( AMD ), Micron ( MU ), and other chip stocks fell.
Markets will get another dose of hyperscaler earnings after the bell on Thursday when Amazon ( AMZN ) reports results. Several other big corporations, including Eli Lilly ( LLY ), Mastercard ( MA ), Intel ( INTC ), Caterpillar ( CAT ), and Anheuser-Busch InBev ( BUD ), will also provide insight into the AI trade and other facets of the economy.
A day after the Fed's interest rate decision, investors will also be treated to inflation data by way of the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) index, which is expected to rise 3.1% on a core basis.
Yahoo Finance's Hamza Shaban reports:
Retail investors are changing the way they trade.
While overall retail volumes are declining , as Goldman Sachs strategist Ben Snider wrote in a recent note, money is shifting away from traditional equities.
Instead, more investors are pouring their funds into options, leveraged ETFs, and prediction markets. Robinhood's ( HOOD ) latest earnings offer a window into the shift .
The online brokerage reported weaker-than-expected profits earlier this week as declining interest income and rising expenses weighed on the company. But it also drew record trading activity in stocks, options, and prediction markets.
Robinhood said revenue from prediction markets increased more than 500% from this time last year, up to $173 million. Customers traded a record 16.4 billion contracts during the past quarter.
Oil dropped as traders weighed fresh diplomatic efforts in the Middle East to avert a potential restart of US military strikes on Iran.
West Texas Intermediate fell toward $102 a barrel, after rising almost 3% in the previous session, while Brent closed near $115. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that Tehran continued to give diplomacy chance, and the Wall Street Journal reported US Vice President JD Vance had reached out to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the nation's top security body.
President Donald Trump told Axios on Wednesday that negotiations were taking place through mediators but stressed he didn't know whether they would bear fruit. "We need to finish the job — either through a deal or another way — we will find out if negotiations can succeed," he was quoted as saying.
Yahoo Finance's Julie Hyman writes:
Anthropic's hotly anticipated S-1 filing finally dropped Monday, providing investors with greater visibility into its financials, ownership structure, and potential risks .
But there are plenty of questions the document didn't answer that will be vital in helping investors decide whether to buy the stock. Some clarity could come before the IPO. Other lingering uncertainties might not be resolved for years.
First, creating short-term suspense, the prospectus contained several prominent omissions that will likely be included in an amended filing before the IPO. They include third quarter financials and details on share-lockup expirations — when insiders are allowed to sell. The expiration schedule currently includes dates but not the number of shares affected.
The most important interim question is where Anthropic shares will be priced. It's tough to decide whether to buy something if you don't know what it costs. Analysts can't get a handle on the public stock's valuation before pricing is announced.

articles.title_orig: Sanrio ends tie-up with Japan drama "Vivant" after criticism in China
articles.title_zh: Sanrio ends tie-up with Japan drama "Vivant" after criticism in China
articles.content_orig:
The company best known for its cute characters cut ties with the drama after strong Chinese criticism of its evocation of wartime torture
In an official statement released on its Japanese website on Thursday, the company acknowledged that the Japanese spy drama contained content that “does not align with the Sanrio Group’s corporate philosophy”.
The controversial series includes scenes depicting Chinese intelligence agents torturing Japanese operatives, prompting China’s state broadcaster CCTV to accuse the show of distorting history and “deliberately smearing” Beijing.
In its statement, Sanrio confirmed that it was ceasing the current collaboration with Vivant – which premiered in 2023 and opened its second season in July – along with all related future projects and promotional campaigns.

Vice President JD Vance has sent a letter to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei seeking to restart peace negotiations, according to multiple reports, but President Trump insists it is a focused outreach intended only to help get medical supplies into Iran.
Mr. Trump has said repeatedly in recent weeks that he is still mulling whether to resume major military operations against Iran or make a peace deal after next week's midterm elections, according to various outlets.
The Wall Street Journal first reported that Vance was engaging directly with Mohsen Rezaei, one of Iran's most powerful hard-liners, in an effort to revive negotiations, citing U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter.
Vance sent the letter to Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' longest-serving former commander, at President Trump's direction, according to The Journal. The initiative seeks to establish whether Washington and Tehran can find common ground to avert a renewed conflict, the paper reported.
According to The New York Times , the letter, sent last week via Qatari mediators and delivered to Rezaei on Sunday, proposed an early meeting between American and Iranian officials, with Vance offering to lead the U.S. negotiating team.
The Times said Rezaei was expected to issue a formal response by Thursday. The letter did not specify a date or location for negotiations, but U.S. and Iranian officials were quoted by the newspaper as saying direct talks could begin as soon as next week in Qatar or Turkey.
According to Axios , Vance's letter explicitly stated that any negotiations aimed at preventing new U.S. military strikes would require discussions on Iran's nuclear program.
Asked Wednesday about Vance's contact with Iranian officials, Mr. Trump told reporters he had not sought to renew peace talks, but "what that is, they [Iran] need help with medical supplies and various things. He [Vance] asked me what I thought and I said, 'If you want to do that that's okay.' Basically it's getting supplies in to help people who are not well."
An official briefed on the diplomacy confirmed to CBS News Wednesday that Qatari mediators had presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the war.
A response is expected from Tehran by the end of the week, most likely Saturday, the official added.
On Wednesday, a senior Iranian official denied Qatar had presented Tehran with a new peace proposal on Sunday, saying instead Qatar had only come with "unacceptable" ideas , Reuters reported.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' (IRGC) said Thursday that three oil tankers exploded and caught fire after striking naval mines while attempting to transit what it described as "the unauthorized southern route" through the Strait of Hormuz.
In a statement, the IRGC Navy's public relations office said the incidents occurred over the past 24 hours, adding that the vessels were subsequently stranded along the southern shores of the strait.
The U.S. has encouraged shippers to use a southern shipping lane through the vital waterway, which President Trump himself declared mine-free at the end of August. Iran insists vessels can only transit the strait through routes it administers closer to its coast in the north of the strait, in coordination with Iranian authorities.
"These oil tankers had switched off all their radar and navigation systems," the IRGC added, referring to a common practice for vessels trying to avoid either U.S. or Iranian-imposed blockades in the strait and surrounding waters.
The vessels, "disregarding warnings from the IRGC Navy, were attempting to exit through the unauthorized southern route of the Strait of Hormuz when they struck naval mines and exploded," the IRGC said.
The IRGC said it held the vessels' owners and crews responsible for using the route that Tehran has warned against for months.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has fired the Pentagon's top military planner, Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, a Pentagon official has told CBS News, after he was accused of leaking classified information related to the Iran war.
Sylvia was removed on Wednesday as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff, becoming the latest in a series of generals to be ousted by Hegseth.
U.S. officials have told several Middle Eastern countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action against Iran after next week's midterm elections – as well as the possibility that Iran will attempt to retaliate against them, two diplomats briefed on the matter told the Associated Press.
President Trump has not made a final decision on whether to carry out new strikes against Iran, the diplomats, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, stressed. He has, however, repeatedly said that he is weighing ordering new military action once the critical Nov. 3 elections are over.
Those threats and the fresh U.S. urgings for allies to prepare for potential retaliation have put the region on alert for a possible return to major operations.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday in a post on X that Tehran "continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed" and is working with mediators to review ideas that Tehran included in a proposal floated last month, which was summarily rejected by Mr. Trump, but which Iran still wants to see used as the basis for a new ceasefire agreement.
The U.S. has told regional allies that a new round of military action could last for just several days, but regional officials are bracing for Iran and its proxy groups to retaliate, which could bring longer-term fighting, the diplomats told the AP.
The allies have also been urged by U.S. officials to take precautionary measures in anticipation that Iran's response would include retaliatory strikes on energy facilities and other crucial infrastructure.

The crew's status wasn't known and there was no damage assessment or report on the incident's environmental impact, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) added.

The United States has responded with a counterblockade of Iranian ports.

"Air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward the Eastern Province," coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki posted on X.
Saudi Arabia has this month come under sustained attack from the Iran-backed Houthis, including a strike on Riyadh's international airport that was the kingdom's deadliest in years.

articles.title_orig: President of the European Central Bank Christine Lagarde to stand down in February
articles.title_zh: President of the European Central Bank Christine Lagarde to stand down in February
articles.content_orig:
European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde will step down from her role on Feb. 7 next year, nearly nine months before her term expires, she announced Thursday.
"It has been a source of great pride to serve this institution. I thank all of those who have supported me on this journey over the past seven years," Lagarde said.
Lagarde has led the central bank since July 2019, steering its policy responses to the Covid-19 pandemic, the Russia-Ukraine war and a series of energy price shocks that sent inflation in the 21-nation euro area above 11%. Her term was due to end in October 2027.
She was given a standing ovation by the Governing Council of the central bank on Thursday.
The announcement came ahead of the ECB's latest monetary policy decision, due later on Thursday, in which it is expected to hold interest rates despite inflation in the 21-nation euro zone hitting a three-year high in September.
European Council President Antonio Costa thanked Lagarde for her "dedication."
"She has provided a steady and determined stewardship, helping to safeguard stability and the resilience of the euro area," Costa said in a statement.
The process of appointing her successor will begin immediately, he added.
Lagarde, born in Paris in 1956, first worked as a high-ranking lawyer before joining the French government. In 2007, she became the first female Finance Minister of a G7 country. She was appointed managing director of the International Monetary Fund in 2011 before joining the ECB.
Lagarde is viewed as a top candidate to become the next chair of the World Economic Forum, according to Financial Times reporting . In recent media interviews , she has suggested she does not plan a run at the French presidency in the 2027 election.
The ECB's leadership is now engaged in talks as the central bank looks to fill a number of senior roles, with chief economist Philip Lane and executive board member Isabel Schnabel also due to step down next year.
Former head of the Netherlands central bank, Klaas Knot, and former head of Spain's central bank, Pablo Hernández de Cos, are widely regarded as top contenders to replace Lagarde.
"Both are excellent candidates," ING's global head of macro Carsten Brzeski told CNBC by email on Thursday.
"Nationality will also matter. While Knot might find more support among Northern European governments, the question is whether De Cos will be supported by the current Spanish government."
"In any case, both would bring a high level of monetary policy expertise to the table. Something that Christine Lagarde had to pick up on when already in office."
Berenberg Chief Economist Holger Schmieding said that as well as the usual issues of monetary policy competence and regional balance, the ECB would need to consider who could deal with potential financial turbulence amid widening spreads in bond yields between member states.
Market participants are debating whether the ECB could be forced to use one of its intervention mechanisms as France faces a mounting sovereign debt crisis , with further uncertainty ahead due to next year's election.
"As a former chair of the G20's Financial Stability Board (FSB), Knot may have an edge in this respect," Schmieding said in a note.
"The European Union is trying to guard itself at least somewhat against the risk that right-wing Marine Le Pen may win the French presidential election in April/May 2027."
"However, the ECB has no mandate and no appetite to fund French fiscal follies. In our view, the ECB would only support France if Paris returns to more sustainable policies," he said.

articles.title_orig: Spain train crash: What we know after two trains crashed with dozens feared dead
articles.title_zh: Spain train crash: What we know after two trains crashed with dozens feared dead
articles.content_orig:
Two trains crashed south of the Spanish capital Madrid on Wednesday morning, on the high-speed line to Seville.
At least 69 people died in the collision, when a state-operated Renfe train went into the back of a stationary train operated by the Iryo company near the town of Urda.
Here is what we know about the crash so far.
The crash happened at 08:53 (07:53 GMT) between municipalities Mora and Orgaz, and about 140km (100 miles) south of Madrid, according to an account given by the Spanish government.
The privately run Iryo train appears to have been stationary on the state-run Renfe train barrelled into the back of it at high speed. Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by a Renfe train "due to causes that are still unknown".
The crash caused some carriages to fall down an embankment.
All train traffic on the line was stopped at stations along the route.
Renfe said services between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia were suspended.
A passenger on board one of the trains told local media there was a heavy impact about 40 minutes into the journey.
Transport minister Óscar Puente said a computer failure at about 08:30 on Wednesday morning led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.
"In the event of a system failure, the control centre takes over," he said, adding it was the control centre that decided to allow the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions.
That decision, Puente said, was made "under inexplicable circumstances". It resulted in the Renfe train crashing into the Iryo train, which was stationary on the tracks some distance ahead.
Audio recordings obtained by Spanish media between train controllers working in Madrid for a rail infrastructure company in Adif in Madrid and the train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move at 08:36 even though another some 25km ahead had stalled.
In one recording, the controller tells the driver of the Renfe train to disconnect and reconnect the LZB mechanism that monitors train speeds, and then resume the journey at normal speed.
"Disconnect and reconnect LZB. Continue your journey and then proceed under [Lateral Signalling Block], at normal speed with normal operation," the control centre operator says to the driver.
The driver replies, "At normal speed?" To which the controller says: "Yes."
Under normal protocols, the driver would be expected to continue moving at a maximum of 40km/h according to their line of sight, and not at normal speed on a track designed for speeds of up to 200km/h.
The Lateral Signaling Block is a back-up or alternative train system used when the automatic signalling or data transmission system fails.
In a second audio recording between the driver of the Iryo train in front and the control centre, the driver says the train "is stationary in front of the entry signal at Urda". After some exchanges, the control centre operator tells the driver to "resume the journey" normally.
The Iryo driver then contacts the control centre again, according to a later recording, saying they cannot start the train. "The train won't allow me to control the [security] system. That's why I am still stopped in front of the entry signal," they say.
The latter recording suggests that the controller had been notified that the Iryo train remained stationary as the Renfe train approached.
More than 540 people were on board both trains.
Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the government of Castilla-La Mancha region, told TVE that one of the trains - managed by the Iryo company - was carrying 146 passengers plus one baby, while the Renfe-managed train had 397 passengers on board.
A former government minister was also among those reported missing.
The Spanish Confederation of Business Organizations (CEOE) posted on X that, Fátima Báñez - who heads the organization's foundation - was on board one of the trains involved in the crash.
More than 100 people were treated for injuries, according to Spanish authorities, and by the next day 50 of them were still in hospital, 15 in a critical condition.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has said "the whole of Spain is grieving" and that "lives have been shattered, families have been torn apart".
"The pain is immense," he said on a visit to the crash site.
The government was "trying to determine what was the origin of this tragedy, of this terrible accident," he added.
"We will get to the bottom of this, and if there has been any negligence, it will come to light.
"If there have been failures in the security system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness."
Opposition conservative leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, whose People's Party leads most opinion polls ahead of 29 November elections, said it was not the day to talk about political responsibility, but insisted "Spain has the right to know what is going on with its infrastructure".
Most Spanish politicians cancelled all public engagements on Wednesday and suspended their election campaign.
However, Santiago Abascal of the far-right Vox refused to take part in what his party described as attempts to "use mourning to silence criticism" of the country's rail infrastructure.
Three days of official mourning began on Thursday.
Spain's royal family posted on X that it was "shocked and concerned" and expressed condolences for the relatives of the deceased and those affected by the crash.
A spokesperson for the EU said the bloc was ready to help Spain if needed.
A huge emergency response was under way with fire crews and helicopters at the scene.
Hospitals in the area suspended planned surgeries as they deal with an influx of patients from the crash, Spanish media have reported.
A blood transfusion centre in Madrid appealed for "urgent" donations. In a post on X, Centro de Transfusión said it made the request "in the face of a possible sudden increase in care needs".
It reported that facilities in Toledo, Ciudad Real and Alcázar de San Juan had cancelled procedures as casualties from the crash begin to arrive.
The Spanish Civil Guard set up bureaus in Madrid, Toledo, Seville and Córdoba to investigate reports of missing persons.
"The top priority is the identification of the missing persons and the taking of DNA samples to be able to locate their relatives," the civil guard wrote in a post on X.
This is the second high-speed rail tragedy in Spain this year.
In January a high-speed train derailed in southern Spain , its rear carriages going into the path of a state-run Renfe train, claiming the lives of 46 people.

articles.title_orig: Why students in ancient China honoured teachers by gifting wild vegetables
articles.title_zh: Why students in ancient China honoured teachers by gifting wild vegetables
articles.content_orig:
Students gifted only water celery or white wormwood, choosing these fragrant plants to symbolise a pure pursuit of knowledge
While it is common for Chinese people to hold banquets for teachers upon graduation as a way of honouring them – a traditional value – in ancient China, students expressed their respect for teachers differently: by presenting them with vegetables.
The tradition began in the Zhou dynasty (1046–256 BC). On the first day of school, students wore blue gowns and brought their teachers wild vegetables they had gathered themselves. They then bowed reverently before memorial tablets honouring ancient sages. The ceremony was followed by a group dance, which also expressed the students’ respect for their teachers and their dedication to their studies.
Not just any vegetables could be presented to teachers on this day. Water celery and white wormwood were preferred because they were seen as clean, fragrant and ethereal, symbolising the students’ pure pursuit of knowledge.

articles.title_zh: Alphabet and Microsoft are on both sides of the AI boom's biggest bills: Chart of the Day
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Wall Street bought Microsoft and sold Alphabet after the two reported quarterly earnings Wednesday night. Both rent computing power to the AI labs and own stakes in them, but this quarter Microsoft cashed in while Alphabet's bets cost it.
Microsoft ( MSFT ) stock rose about 2% after hours, while Alphabet ( GOOGL , GOOG ) fell over 9%, on track for its worst day since October 2023, after its sales came up short .
For Microsoft, the labs show up as sales. OpenAI paid it $10 billion in the quarter that ended in September, according to Microsoft's quarterly filing. That's about 11% of Microsoft's $92 billion in revenue, and more than its Xbox and Windows businesses brought in combined.
Some of that money is still owed. OpenAI's unpaid bills to Microsoft rose to about $7 billion from $6 billion three months earlier. Microsoft also owns about 24% of the ChatGPT maker, but the stake barely moved its profit this time.
The order book cooled, too. Microsoft's backlog — revenue customers have signed up for, but Microsoft hasn't yet booked — slipped to about $677 billion, and new bookings fell 12% from a year earlier. CFO Amy Hood blamed "large Azure commitments in the prior year" for the tough comparison.
Alphabet's bets on the labs worked the other way. Its stakes in other companies, including roughly 14% of Anthropic and a piece of SpaceX ( SPCX ), supplied about $6 of its $9.11 in per-share profit in the second quarter.
This time they cost it. A nearly $9 billion loss on those holdings cut earnings by $0.55 a share, to $2.12. CFO Anat Ashkenazi said on the call that the loss came "primarily" from SpaceX, whose stock dropped about 12% during the quarter.
Alphabet is also footing the bill to build. It spent $51 billion on data centers and equipment in the quarter, more than double a year earlier, and burned about $9 billion in free cash flow — the cash left after those investments — for a second straight quarter. Microsoft generated about $19 billion and said it expects to stay positive this fiscal year.
To cover the gap, Alphabet bought back no stock, sold about $29 billion of bonds and $12 billion of new shares, and nearly tripled its long-term debt this year to about $125 billion. Meta ( META ) took a similar route with its nearly $100 billion stock sale .
The payoff is showing up in Google Cloud, where revenue doubled to about $31 billion and the backlog of signed contracts rose to $561 billion from $514 billion three months earlier. Anthropic has committed at least $115 billion to Google for computing power, according to its IPO filing, about a fifth of that backlog by Yahoo Finance calculations.
The next swing could come from Anthropic itself. Its IPO could start trading as soon as Nov. 16 , and once it does, Alphabet's stake gets valued at the market price each quarter. At the reported $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion valuation, that could turn the drag back into a windfall by year-end.
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella doesn't want to lean on the labs forever. Asked on the call where Azure's AI growth is coming from, he said he's after breadth, not "four customers who buy a lot of capacity from you and you can show a few quarters of growth."
"That's not a business as far as I'm concerned," he said.

articles.title_orig: Israelis await final election results as claim of foreign interference emerges
articles.title_zh: Israelis await final election results as claim of foreign interference emerges
articles.content_orig:
In a political career that has spanned more than three decades, Benjamin Netanyahu has been written off too many times to count, only to prove the obituaries were penned prematurely. Israel’s election results this week appear to give the prime minister’s opponents a chance to end his run, but in the country’s ruthless political system, it’s no guarantee.
By Wednesday night, most votes had been counted. But there is no clear winner for Israel’s top post, setting up weeks — possibly months — in which Netanyahu’s political survival remains on the line.
With the vote counting nearing its conclusion, Netanyahu’s Likud party remains the largest party in the 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset, with an estimated 26 seats. But his right-wing bloc has lost its majority, set to win only 53 seats, short of the 61-seat majority needed to govern.
Netanyahu hasn’t won. But he hasn’t lost, either — at least not yet. Now, he has to stop his rivals from building their own government, and he may survive again.
On paper, the opposition holds roughly 67 seats, but that arithmetic is fractured by ideological, national and personal rivalries. Netanyahu’s main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot , won 21 seats, but the Jewish opposition parties total only 48, well short of victory. To reach 61, they would need the support of two Arab parties, Raam and the Joint List, which are projected to win a record 19 seats between them. Analysts say that record turnout by Arabs or Palestinian citizens of Israel was in part a backlash to four years of a far-right national security minister under whom crime in the Arab community soared, and members of the community have blamed the trend on negligent policing. They have also been affected by a rise in racism following October 7 and Israel’s war in Gaza — and have been highly critical of settler violence, all factors that could have mobilized them to vote.
This is where the math gets complicated. Raam is an Islamist party that draws heavily from Israel’s Bedouin community. Its leader, Mansour Abbas, became the first Arab politician to join an Israeli government following the country’s 2021 election. The Joint List, projected to be the bigger Arab party, combines several smaller parties: the Communist Hadash, secularist Taal and nationalist Balad factions.
On Wednesday, Yair Golan, leader of the left-wing Democrats party, called on his partners to count the Arab parties as part of the bloc, rejecting what he called Netanyahu’s “racist division between Jewish and Arab votes.” But two of Eisenkot’s right-wing allies, Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Liberman, have opposed any government that depends on the Arab parties. (They have not issued a statement on the issue since polls closed.)
The Joint List said Wednesday that it was ready for political cooperation and willing to do “do everything in its power to bring Netanyahu’s rule to an end.”
A source close to Netanyahu said his main post-election goal is to delegitimize and therefore prevent the Jewish-Arab political cooperation that could send him home.
“He is very concerned about a minority government,” the source said. Netanyahu even plans to pressure individual opposition lawmakers not to cooperate with the Arab parties. After campaigning against them throughout the election, Likud issued a statement Wednesday accusing the Arab parties of “stealing the election” through bribery, threats, violence and forgery, echoing election fraud claims from his closest ally, US President Donald Trump. The Central Elections Committee said Wednesday it was examining the complaint, but the committee had already dismissed thousands of complaints from the different parties on election day.
Netanyahu plans to “neutralize this possibility by all means,” the source told CNN, “including launching an attack on Iran or enlisting President Trump to intervene in Israeli politics on his behalf.”
The opposition fears that Netanyahu could use a security crisis to stall or block a new government. Before the election, Netanyahu had pressed Trump to launch a joint attack on Iran, but Washington held off, partly because Israeli military chief of staff Eyal Zamir warned it could disrupt the vote. An Israeli security source told CNN the operational plans are ready and awaiting Trump’s approval, possibly after the US midterms.
“There is no way to know what Netanyahu will do,” an opposition source told CNN. “We are aware that he may try to push for another escalation.” Another source said that Netanyahu “will do everything he can not to leave the prime minister’s office, including domestic and external chaos.”
Eisenkot, a former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff, called on Israel’s security chiefs Tuesday night to remember that “Netanyahu is a caretaker prime minister, without a mandate and without public confidence.” Speaking to supporters shortly after exit polls were published, Eisenkot declared that the public “has chosen change.”
In his first reaction to the updated results since Tuesday night’s speech, Eisenkot said he remains committed to “bringing change to Israel.”
The numbers can still change. By Wednesday evening, the Central Elections Committee is expected to finish counting most ballots. Attention now turns to double-envelope ballots from home by soldiers, prisoners, hospital patients and staff, diplomats abroad and voters with disabilities. The committee estimates there are between 430,000 and 480,000 double envelopes, enough for over 10 seats. They are counted separately in a special verification process, with final results expected Thursday.
Then the political maneuvering begins in earnest.
The next step runs through President Isaac Herzog, whose post-election role is pivotal. His job here is to consult with all elected parties on the candidate they recommend as prime minister, before picking the one he believes is most likely to secure a 61-seat majority. This is not necessarily the leader of the largest party but the one with the most plausible path to a coalition.
Eisenkot is likely to collect more recommendations than Netanyahu, since the Arab parties are expected to back him.
Then the clock starts ticking.
The chosen candidate has 28 days — and a possible 14-day extension — to negotiate with other parties over cabinet posts, budgets and policies in order to form a government. If he fails, the mandate passes to another candidate for another four weeks. If he fails, too, the Knesset gets a short window to put forward an alternative candidate. If that fails, the country goes to automatic elections.
Netanyahu, as caretaker prime minister, has a built-in advantage. If Eisenkot receives the mandate first — and fails — all he needs to do is wait for his time to pass. And if Israel finds itself headed for new elections, Netanyahu will remain caretaker for months.
Eisenkot isn’t out of options entirely.
Even without forming a government, the opposition could still leverage its parliamentary majority to replace the Knesset speaker and other key positions. That could limit Netanyahu’s ability to govern and even enable the opposition to advance legislation.
But Eisenkot, a retired lieutenant general, isn’t on his preferred battlefield. Netanyahu’s coalition remains incredibly loyal, and he doesn’t have to worry in any real way about defections. The same cannot be said for Eisenkot. His diverse coalition is far less ideologically aligned, and even the tiniest step could splinter the bloc and send the country back to elections.
For now, the focus is on Herzog, whose role is even more important given the current deadlock. With neither bloc holding a clear majority, he may try to push Netanyahu and Eisenkot to form a unity government.
“We must do everything to avoid another round of elections,” Herzog said Wednesday. He called on party leaders to come to consultations with an “open mind.”

articles.title_orig: Why Microsoft stock isn't getting crushed like Google stock after its earnings report
articles.title_zh: Why Microsoft stock isn't getting crushed like Google stock after its earnings report
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
While Alphabet's ( GOOGL ) stock is getting crushed on Thursday after earnings, Microsoft ( MSFT ) is getting a pass.
Another way of saying it: Microsoft shares aren't trading down in sympathy.
And there is one simple reason why this is the case.
Microsoft's quarter is being seen as one of higher-than-expected growth that is sustainable, while Alphabet's quarter was sluggish and hinted at slowing growth rates in coming quarters.
Microsoft's Azure sales growth came in about 300 basis points above analyst estimates. Overall sales for the important cloud business grew 48%, excluding currency fluctuations.
Execs guided to 49% to 50% Azure sales growth in the current quarter, ahead of consensus estimates by four percentage points.
The company's capex came in about $5 billion below estimates, and other parts of the business showed sales upside.
Sales and earnings for the quarter came in ahead of analyst forecasts.
"Net/net, these results increase our confidence in the company's ability to sustain mid/upper-teens revenue growth and that strong cost of goods sold/expense operational efficiencies should be supportive of expanding operating margins," said stifel analyst Brad Reback.
Microsoft shares rose 4% in pre-market trading.
Alphabet shares tanked 10% in pre-market trading after a third quarter that could best be characterized as a letdown, both on its own and versus Microsoft.
First, Google's search business notched sales of $63.4 billion, below the $64.9 billion expected. The miss fueled fears Google's search empire is being chipped away by the likes of Claude and ChatGPT, despite massive investment by Google.
Second, Google posted negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion versus a Wall Street estimate for negative $3.5 billion. In a market getting jittery about negative free cash flow at Big Tech (see the reaction to Meta's ( META ) results last week, when it also had negative free cash flow for the first time in years), Google's print stunk up the joint.
"Alphabet's 3Q results reinforced concerns we had heading into the print, re: Search is decelerating and margins have peaked near-term. This could create an air pocket over the next 1-2 quarters as investors await signs for whether this is transitory or structural," KeyBanc analyst Justin Patterson said.

articles.title_orig: An ‘Endless’ Cruise Around the World Is Suspended, Leaving Passengers Stranded
articles.title_zh: An ‘Endless’ Cruise Around the World Is Suspended, Leaving Passengers Stranded
articles.content_orig:
A US cruise ship MV. Odyssey docked at Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville southern Cambodia, Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
SIHANOUKVILLE, Cambodia — A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year journey in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.
The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to "make the Odyssey your permanent home," with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting around $230,000.
For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.
The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials. It has a 650-passenger capacity.
Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 have reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran. The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.
Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.
"We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses," Villa Vie Residences said in a statement issued Tuesday. "Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees" while it tries to restructure.
"The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements," it said.
Passengers, however, said they received no support and had to make their own arrangements after being given seven hours notice on Tuesday to disembark. Some were devastated and expressed hope a new company could rescue the venture so life at sea can continue.
Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming, said they bought a window cabin and had expected to sail for years. They boarded the ship 17 months ago in Panama.
A couple passenger from a U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, Paul Montoya, left, stands for an interview with his wife, Lynn Motoya, at the Independence Hotel in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
Paul praised the concept of residential cruising but said the shipowner lacked the expertise to make the business financially sustainable. While rising fuel costs had been cited publicly as the reason for the suspension, he said the company had already been struggling. Changes to itinerary, unreliable internet access and declining food quality had pushed many residents to leave the ship in recent months, he said.
Lynn said residents were repeatedly asked to contribute additional money for fuel and other expenses, including a fresh call to raise funds for fuel to get out of Cambodia. She said the crew members were also not paid.
"We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything," she said. "We had hopes but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole through mismanagement."
The company could not immediately be contacted for comment.
Yet for some, even the financial and logistical turmoil couldn't outweigh the extraordinary experience of traveling the world and living at sea.
Carol Larson, 69, and her sister Crystal Lavering, 72, occupied separate cabins aboard the ship for 18 months. The siblings, from California, described the suspension as heartbreaking, and hoped the cruise would be resuscitated.
A sibling passenger from a U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, Carol Larson, 69, left, stands for an interview with her sister, Crystal Lavering, at the Independence Hotel in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
"I hope there is a movement for the residents to buy the ship and I am hoping that goes through because it's a dream to live on the ship and I don't want it to end," Larson said.
Lavering said her health improved during her time on the ship, and that she didn't need to use a cane to walk anymore. "You come to this ship to live … it's just sad that it's all over."
Larson bought her cabin for $120,000, paid in installments, in addition to monthly maintenance fees, under a plan that had promised the possibility of living aboard for up to 15 years. She said she blamed U.S. President Donald Trump for the ship's woes as fuel costs spiked due to the Iran war, in addition to poor management. But she said she didn't regret her investment.
"Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk. From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money's worth … I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising," she said.
The ship arrived in Sihanoukville last Friday and was scheduled to depart Wednesday, according to a statement from Long Dimanche, the deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk province. He said it was now expected to refuel and depart Cambodia on Saturday, but the ship's operator has not yet publicly confirmed any date.
A U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, docks at the Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, late Wednesday evening, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before being becalmed by the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.
Its current cruise, originally intended to last 3 1/2 years, began in October 2024 in Belfast, Northern Ireland, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise had been tentatively scheduled to end in August 2030.
The Odyssey is not the first cruise ship Sihanoukville has hosted in crisis.
In February 2020, the MS Westerdam was allowed to dock in Cambodia after being turned away at five ports in other nations because of fears of COVID-19, which just a month earlier had started to spread from China. It carried 1,455 passengers, more than 600 of them American citizens.
After being stranded at sea for two weeks, Cambodia's then-Prime Minister Hun Sen allowed it to dock for what he said were humanitarian reasons. Cambodia won plaudits as passengers were welcomed ashore and arrangements were made for them to fly home.

Alphabet ( GOOGL , GOOG ) profit took a hit from an unusual place: its stakes in other companies.

The filing that shows which stakes fell isn't out yet, but SpaceX stock dropped about 12% during the quarter.

articles.title_zh: North Korea fires missiles as row over landmine blast intensifies
articles.content_orig:
North Korea has fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast into the Sea of Japan, according to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS), less than a week after Seoul proposed talks over a growing border dispute.
The missiles were launched at about 12:30pm (03:30 GMT) on Thursday from an area around Wonsan on North Korea’s eastern coast, the JCS said in a statement.
Japan’s Defence Ministry separately confirmed the launch of what it said could be a ballistic missile that fell outside the country’s Exclusive Economic Zone, Tokyo-based Kyodo News reported.
The launch comes against the backdrop of growing tensions over a landmine explosion that injured three South Korean soldiers in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), a heavily fortified border between the two Koreas, on September 21.
A joint South Korea-United Nations investigation earlier this month concluded that North Korea had planted the landmines more than a year ago,with Seoul calling for an apology.
Pyongyang rejected the finding, sending a letter to the UN Security Council (UNSC) this week accusing Seoul of fabricating the explosion.
The North Korean permanent representative to the UN, Kim Song, wrote about the “provocation the ROK [Republic of Korea] committed by groundlessly shifting the blame for the dubious ‘mine explosion incident’”, warning that violations of the country’s sovereignty could trigger self-defence.
Song told the UNSC that South Korea’s claims were a “farce to evade the responsibility for the ever-escalating tensions on the Korean peninsula”.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, labelled South Korean demands for an apology as “despicable” while separately rejecting an offer of medical equipment from Seoul.
South Korea has proposed military talks with its neighbour in a bid to calm the situation.
Seoul said last Friday that it had invited Pyongyang to discuss restoring communication channels. The offer was made as military activity on the border increases.
It remains unclear whether North Korea would agree to talks. Leader Kim has taken a hardline approach towards Seoul and suspended virtually all dialogue and cooperation with the South in recent years.
The ratcheting tensions come as United States President Donald Trump’s recent overtures to Pyongyang have raised concerns that US ally Seoul could be sidelined in potential nuclear talks involving the North.
Pyongyang launched several short-range ballistic missiles a day after Trump suggested he might meet Kim this year.

articles.title_orig: A U.S. cruise ship suspends a global voyage due to fuel costs, stranding 200 passengers
articles.title_zh: A U.S. cruise ship suspends a global voyage due to fuel costs, stranding 200 passengers
articles.content_orig:
A US cruise ship MV. Odyssey docked at Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville southern Cambodia, Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
SIHANOUKVILLE, Cambodia — A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year journey in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.
The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to "make the Odyssey your permanent home," with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting around $230,000.
For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.
The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials. It has a 650-passenger capacity.
Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 have reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran. The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.
Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.
"We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses," Villa Vie Residences said in a statement issued Tuesday. "Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees" while it tries to restructure.
"The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements," it said.
Passengers, however, said they received no support and had to make their own arrangements after being given seven hours notice on Tuesday to disembark. Some were devastated and expressed hope a new company could rescue the venture so life at sea can continue.
Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming, said they bought a window cabin and had expected to sail for years. They boarded the ship 17 months ago in Panama.
A couple passenger from a U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, Paul Montoya, left, stands for an interview with his wife, Lynn Motoya, at the Independence Hotel in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
Paul praised the concept of residential cruising but said the shipowner lacked the expertise to make the business financially sustainable. While rising fuel costs had been cited publicly as the reason for the suspension, he said the company had already been struggling. Changes to itinerary, unreliable internet access and declining food quality had pushed many residents to leave the ship in recent months, he said.
Lynn said residents were repeatedly asked to contribute additional money for fuel and other expenses, including a fresh call to raise funds for fuel to get out of Cambodia. She said the crew members were also not paid.
"We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything," she said. "We had hopes but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole through mismanagement."
The company could not immediately be contacted for comment.
Yet for some, even the financial and logistical turmoil couldn't outweigh the extraordinary experience of traveling the world and living at sea.
Carol Larson, 69, and her sister Crystal Lavering, 72, occupied separate cabins aboard the ship for 18 months. The siblings, from California, described the suspension as heartbreaking, and hoped the cruise would be resuscitated.
A sibling passenger from a U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, Carol Larson, 69, left, stands for an interview with her sister, Crystal Lavering, at the Independence Hotel in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
"I hope there is a movement for the residents to buy the ship and I am hoping that goes through because it's a dream to live on the ship and I don't want it to end," Larson said.
Lavering said her health improved during her time on the ship, and that she didn't need to use a cane to walk anymore. "You come to this ship to live … it's just sad that it's all over."
Larson bought her cabin for $120,000, paid in installments, in addition to monthly maintenance fees, under a plan that had promised the possibility of living aboard for up to 15 years. She said she blamed U.S. President Donald Trump for the ship's woes as fuel costs spiked due to the Iran war, in addition to poor management. But she said she didn't regret her investment.
"Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk. From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money's worth … I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising," she said.
The ship arrived in Sihanoukville last Friday and was scheduled to depart Wednesday, according to a statement from Long Dimanche, the deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk province. He said it was now expected to refuel and depart Cambodia on Saturday, but the ship's operator has not yet publicly confirmed any date.
A U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, docks at the Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, late Wednesday evening, Oct. 28, 2026. Heng Sinith/AP hide caption
Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before being becalmed by the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.
Its current cruise, originally intended to last 3 1/2 years, began in October 2024 in Belfast, Northern Ireland, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise had been tentatively scheduled to end in August 2030.
The Odyssey is not the first cruise ship Sihanoukville has hosted in crisis.
In February 2020, the MS Westerdam was allowed to dock in Cambodia after being turned away at five ports in other nations because of fears of COVID-19, which just a month earlier had started to spread from China. It carried 1,455 passengers, more than 600 of them American citizens.
After being stranded at sea for two weeks, Cambodia's then-Prime Minister Hun Sen allowed it to dock for what he said were humanitarian reasons. Cambodia won plaudits as passengers were welcomed ashore and arrangements were made for them to fly home.

articles.title_orig: Mum of critically ill baby denied hospital food as she wasn't breastfeeding
articles.title_zh: Mum of critically ill baby denied hospital food as she wasn't breastfeeding
articles.content_orig:
A first-time mum was denied hospital meals while her baby was "fighting for her life" because she was not breastfeeding.
Sophie Price, 22, was "shocked" when staff refused to give her a meal while her daughter Florence was being treated on a paediatric ward at Grange University Hospital in Cwmbran, Torfaen.
Despite giving birth in the hospital five days earlier, she was told she was no longer classed as a patient as she was not breastfeeding, so she would not be provided with meals.
Aneurin Bevan health board said it was "sorry to hear about Sophie's experience" and was "committed to supporting families throughout their child's stay".
"It was just an awful experience. I just needed a hot meal to keep going for my daughter," said Sophie, from Newport.
Her family said they spent more than £1,000 on food from the canteen and takeaway meals during their three-week stay at the hospital while Florence was treated.
The health board said mothers are provided with meals while under the care of hospital maternity services as both them and their baby are classed as patients, whether they are breastfeeding or not.
But on paediatric wards, only the child is classed as the patient, however the hospital's policy is to provide breastfeeding mums with meals as this directly supports the baby's feeding and nutrition.
For babies who are formula-fed, the health board said formula was "provided as needed" by the hospital, but Sophie said she was told she would need to bring it in herself.
Sophie had only left the hospital - which earlier this week denied online claims it was "dangerous" and "dreadful" - for 24 hours before she and her husband Ryli Price had to return when they realised Florence was not able to breathe and the "colour started to drain from her".
"Florence started to make some really harsh grunting sounds, it sounded like a death rattle coming from her chest up into her mouth," she said.
Sophie ran into the A&E department screaming "she's not breathing" and credited the quick response of medical staff who helped save her daughter's life.
Florence was diagnosed with bronchiolitis , rhinoviruses - which causes the common cold - and a blood infection, which meant her lungs could not operate on their own.
She was placed on a machine that pumped air into her lungs via a mask.
Sophie said despite being "hungry and exhausted" she was denied a meal while her daughter was "in intensive care fighting for her life".
"Imagine being in a hospital with your seriously ill baby on breathing support monitors, overwhelmed with worry, anxiety and stress, only to be told you aren't entitled to a meal because you're formula feeding instead of breastfeeding," she said.
Sophie said she was bleeding through her clothes and "in a lot of pain" as her hips had to be put back in place after being dislocated during childbirth.
She also had a build-up of fluid in her feet called oedema , adding: "My feet, they were the size of elephant trunks to the point where I couldn't even walk from the one corridor to the next."
Sophie said she and Ryli were told Florence may need to be induced into a coma at any point and it was "so touch-and-go the whole time".
At one point, Sophie said she realised she had not eaten for about 28 hours and remembered seeing a food trolley being brought round to mums on the ward.
She said: "I remember them saying to me 'oh hi mum, hope you're OK, are you hungry?' And me saying 'oh yeah, I'm absolutely starving, I haven't eaten in ages. What have you got'?'"
Sophie was asked if she was breastfeeding, which she had not been able to do after the first 24 hours of Florence's life as she was no longer taking to her breast milk.
She explained this to staff and said Florence was being given formula, only to be told she was not able to have any food,
"I remember just being so shocked. It was so horrific," Sophie said, adding she already felt "disappointed" at being unable to breastfeed.
Due to her husband's paternity leave coming to an end, Sophie said she had "never been in such a vulnerable situation" and relied on family members to finish work and bring her food while she stayed at Florence's bedside.
Sophie's mother contacted the hospital about the issue, so it continued providing formula for Florence.
Sophie called the policy "outdated" and said it discriminated against formula-feeding mothers "who are doing their very best in difficult circumstances".
She thinks all hospitals should provide meals for mothers, regardless of how they are feeding their babies.
The health board thanked Sophie for her feedback and said it understood "how difficult and stressful it can be for parents when their child is in hospital".
It added: "Where parents are unable to access the hospital canteen, have limited support, or are unable to leave their child's bedside, ward teams can provide a selection of basic food items and refreshments to help meet immediate needs.
"Parents can also access a discounted hospital meal through a ward voucher scheme and where a family is experiencing financial hardship, support can be discussed with the ward team.
"Requests are considered on a case-by-case basis to ensure help is provided fairly and appropriately, taking account of the family's circumstances and the needs of the child."

articles.title_orig: Ofcom outlines age check methods ahead of social media ban for under-16s
articles.title_zh: Ofcom outlines age check methods ahead of social media ban for under-16s
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — Enforcement of the U.K.’s upcoming social media ban for under-16s will probably require older teens to show a form of photo ID, according to the U.K.’s online safety regulator Ofcom.
In a government-commissioned report, Ofcom said it had identified just four methods that are “highly effective” at determining whether a user is 16 or over — while noting that “the risk of circumvention cannot be entirely eliminated, and some children will succeed in bypassing age checks.”
The advice comes after the U.K. government vowed to take a tougher approach than Australia to enforcing its ban — due to come into force next year — by requiring platforms to use “highly effective age assurance” to identify underage users.
It will inform regulations to implement the ban which ministers have said they aim to introduce to parliament this year.
Three of the methods identified by Ofcom — photo ID matching, using a digital ID service, or banking-based checks — require a passport or driving license at some stage, while the fourth, facial age estimation, may in some cases need to be followed by a supplementary check using one of the other methods because of a high margin of error at younger ages.
“This ban will shape the future of children’s lives online, so it’s important to get it right,” Ofcom CEO Melanie Dawes said.
While the age checks would involve processing of personal data, “available methods can be delivered in a way that protects users’ privacy and complies with data protection law,” Ofcom said.
It also said social media platforms should take steps to mitigate circumvention, like enabling users to report suspected underage accounts, and using age inference technology to spot activity from users who may be underage.
The regulator said it will consult on further guidance for platforms once regulations to implement the social media ban are laid.

articles.content_orig:

Hundreds of World War I -era bombs, grenades and artillery shells have been uncovered by the melting of ice in Italy’s Dolomite mountains, the Italian army reports.
Weapons used by the Italian and Austrian armies during the bitterly fought White War in the region, were found in September after a period of sustained glacial ice melt.
The latest finds follow an even bigger tranche of ordnance discovered during the melting over the summer.
In a statement, Italian Army officials said: "As the ice retreats, history resurfaces - and with it, dangers from the past. More than a century later, the mountains continue to yield unexploded ordnance from the Great War."
It's expected that as climate change further melts the Dolomites glaciers , more of the White War's dangerous legacy will emerge.
The officials added: "These complex operations-carried out amidst melting glaciers, steep slopes, and high-altitude terrain-demand a high level of technical expertise and experience.
"Clearing these areas means eliminating hidden dangers and making the trails-frequented every year by mountaineers, hikers, and tourists-safer."
The "White War" was fought between Italian and Austro-Hungarian forces in the freezing, rugged mountain terrain between 1915 and 1918. It included some of the most horrific conditions of the First World War, as troops dug into defensive positions and endured extreme cold amid snow-covered peaks, glaciers and steep mountain slopes.
Hikers reported several sightings of unexploded bombs during the summer, mainly around Canal San Bovo in the Primiero Valley, in the eastern Trentino region.
The Italian army subsequently carried out searches across several high-altitude areas of Trentino-Alto Adige, where retreating glaciers and melting snow have exposed wartime explosives.
Recent operations have focused on the Care Alto and Vedretta di Lares areas of the Adamello-Brenta region in Trento, as well as Val Martello and the Stelvio area in Bolzano.
The army said munitions had also been found at Cima Tre Cannoni and along the edges of the Livrio glacier.
The army said the work aimed to make mountain environments safer for mountaineers, hikers and tourists.
The White War was fought at high altitude, where troops endured extreme cold and faced the challenges of snow-covered peaks, glaciers and steep mountain slopes.
More than a century later, the retreat of glaciers is exposing remnants of the conflict, including unexploded ordnance that can pose a danger to people exploring the mountains.
The army said the risks were not always immediately visible and tended to increase with altitude.
Its campaign to locate and neutralise unexploded munitions in the region is continuing as melting ice reveals further wartime remains.

The Zelda -themed Switch 2 is out this week, and Walmart has reportedly cancelled some pre-orders at the last minute.
As highlighted by Kotaku , some buyers have apparently received a message from Walmart notifying them that their pre-order has been cancelled as the item is now out of stock. They won't be charged, but this information was only shared a day before the expected arrival, so they're no longer getting a system.
Unfortunately, there are similar stories in the past about preorders being cancelled like this. Some individuals have reached out to customer service reps , with Walmart supposedly confirming it "oversold" pre-orders.
Here's one of the many customer responses to Walmart's cancellation of pre-orders:
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 854k
"This is unethical sales practice. They shouldn't allow pre-orders beyond what they can stock. This denied their competitors a sale and denied an excited customer a chance at limited edition merch. I'll try again elsewhere but think consumers should be aware."
Although the system is still "out of stock", new listings on Walmart are now showing up for higher prices on its website. As Kotaku notes, the prices attached to these listings may be "set by a third-party seller using Walmart".
While this update from Walmart is no doubt frustrating for customers who pre-ordered from this retailer, Nintendo has reiterated on a few occasions now how restocks for the Zelda-themed Switch 2 are on the way. So there might still be other ways of securing this limited edition unit.
Website Vooks.net also reports the official Nintendo Store in Australia has received additional Zelda Switch 2 stock this week.

articles.title_orig: Weil Gotshal, Once a Legal Powerhouse, Plans to Dissolve
articles.title_zh: Weil Gotshal, Once a Legal Powerhouse, Plans to Dissolve
articles.content_orig:
Leaders at Weil, Gotshal & Manges, the nearly century-old law firm that worked for companies from the Lehman Brothers to General Motors, recommended on Wednesday that the firm shut down.
“Following a careful review of strategic alternatives, the Firm’s Management Committee has recommended to the partnership that the Firm pursue an orderly wind-down,” a Weil spokesperson said in a statement Wednesday.
The firm’s partners are expected to vote on the recommendation “in the coming days,” according to the statement. Equity partners hold stakes in law firms and can vote on company matters.
For over 90 years, the law firm was well-known through Wall Street for steering high-profile corporate litigation such as bankruptcies and mergers. Weil advised the Lehman Brothers during the 2008 financial crisis, and the firm claims it brought General Motors out of bankruptcy in “just 40 days.”
The firm said it guided debtors such as Enron, whose 2001 bankruptcy filing was the largest in American history at the time. It also advised Microsoft’s $68.7 billion acquisition of Activision Blizzard as well as AT&T’s acquisition of DirecTV .
The firm had been mired by an exodus of prominent partners, largely driven by competition from rivals, legal news outlet Law.com earlier reported . And a potential merger with another law firm, Willkie Farr, fell through this year.
Weil is announcing its closure without filing for bankruptcy.
The news sent shockwaves through the Big Law industry, which has been going through its own changes. Big mergers and acquisitions have led to more competition for top talent – and then there’s the looming dread of artificial intelligence.
Weil was founded in 1931 and employs approximately 1,200 lawyers in offices from New York to Munich to Hong Kong, according to its website. The firm did not announce plans for its employees or office spaces on Wednesday.

articles.title_orig: High-speed train crash in Spain leaves at least 68 dead, dozens injured, officials say
articles.title_zh: High-speed train crash in Spain leaves at least 68 dead, dozens injured, officials say
articles.content_orig:
A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped in central Spain , derailing two cars and killing at least 68 people Wednesday morning, according to local authorities.
The regional government of Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people were receiving medical treatment at hospitals. Rescue workers continue searching the wreckage for survivors and bodies.
The crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo, according to Spain's rail system operator ADIF. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.
Padilla told state broadcaster TVE the accident was between two high-speed trains heading in the same direction from Madrid to Seville and that one ran into the tail of the other while it was stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track.
The accident involved a train from Spain's state-owned RENFE company and the private rail company IRYO. Trains from those two companies were also involved in a deadly crash in January. Padilla said 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers were in the IRYO train.
"Today all of Spain is grieving," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said from the crash site, where he announced that his government would declare three days of national mourning.
Sánchez called for increased safety measures to restore confidence in a high-speed rail system that was once a source of national pride.
"It is unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year," said Sánchez, who faces a national election on Nov. 29.
Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente said the crash was caused by what he called the "inexplicable" order from a central command center for Spain's trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.
Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. But the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stopped IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.
Puente said the train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a "stop signal" active on that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed.
Authorities were still studying information to see how fast the train was going, but it could have been at 200 kph (124 mph) for that stretch of the track, Puente said.
"I am not attributing responsibility to anyone, I am just stating the facts," Puente said.
The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left carriages shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.
Spanish Health Minister Mónica García said that emergency workers were focused on rescuing survivors and bodies from the most damaged train cars.
"It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy," García said.
One passenger said, "We were all thrown into the air." He said he was "reasonably OK" but that his friend was in much worse condition.
Passenger Ignacio Relaño was traveling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the IRYO.
"We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact," he said. "The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook."
Another passenger recounted to Cadena Ser radio how she felt the train slam on the brakes and was thrown forward in her seat, breaking the small table in front of her. She said she saw body parts and trapped people covered in blood.
The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galán, told Spanish state broadcaster TVE that civil protection authorities had asked his town hall to prepare a sports pavilion to attend to passengers.
In January, 45 people died in southern Spain when a train jumped the track and hit an oncoming train. The crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people. The January incident shook the confidence the European country has in its extensive high-speed rail network.

articles.title_orig: Inside India newsletter: New Delhi approves $22 billion in military spending amid China border tensions
articles.title_zh: Inside India newsletter: New Delhi approves $22 billion in military spending amid China border tensions
articles.content_orig:
Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from Singapore.
Welcome to the latest edition of " Inside India " — your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy.
India, the world's fifth-largest military spender, shares a contentious relationship with two of its nuclear-armed neighbors — China and Pakistan. Last year, New Delhi carried out military strikes against alleged terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan, and last week an Indian official confirmed some border clashes with China.
As tensions at its borders simmer, India this week announced plans to spend billions of dollars on procuring modern warfare equipment. From whom will it get the goods?
Any thoughts on today's newsletter? Share them with the team.
The world's second-largest arms importer, India, is pouring billions of dollars into modernizing its military as it seeks to counter the technological advancements of neighboring China, with whom it shares an uneasy peace.
Last week, an Indian military official said that confrontations with Chinese soldiers were ongoing across several locations along the country's north-eastern border.
Shatrujeet Singh Kapoor, the director general of a division of India's central armed forces, the Indo-Tibetan Border Police, also called China the "biggest adversary" and urged for modernization of defense equipment. "It will be difficult to compete with China using traditional methods," Kapoor said.
Following Kapoor's comments, India approved spending 2.12 trillion rupees ($22 billion) to modernize its defense equipment on Monday. The country plans to spend on long-range kamikaze drones, surveillance and strike systems, counter-drone technologies, short-range air defense, artillery, helicopters and naval platforms.
Experts told CNBC that New Delhi increasingly views Beijing as a threat, especially given the Sino-Pakistan military ties, and the latest purchases were aimed at bridging the technological gap with China.
A spokesperson for India's foreign ministry said on Friday that "the situation in the India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns." Beijing responded, saying it "strictly abides by the relevant agreements and common understandings reached between the two countries."
India's military policies are largely driven by its long-standing conflict with Pakistan, and an "increasing perception of China as a threat," Pieter Wezeman, senior researcher at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, told CNBC.
According to a SIPRI report earlier this year, 61% of Chinese arms exports were supplied to Pakistan between 2021 and 2025.
India's latest weapons purchases will involve importing components and technology from South Korea for the artillery, engines and avionics from France for the helicopters, and drones from the U.S. and Israel, Wezeman said.
Collaboration with Russia and Japan could also be on the cards, given India's need for a technological upgrade.
Since April, India has greenlighted military spending totaling 3.7 trillion rupees, which is more than 50% of the 6.73 trillion rupee worth of approvals — a 10-year high — in the financial year ended March 2026, Citi said in a report on Tuesday.
While New Delhi has said it plans to procure 82% of the defense equipment from local industries, foreign companies are likely to play a key role in providing technology crucial for military modernization.
Foreign partnerships remain important for technologies that India does not yet produce independently, Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at strategic advisory firm Teneo, told CNBC. India relies on imported technologies for specialized components such as aircraft engines, propulsion systems, sensors and electronic subsystems, he explained.
"American, Israeli, and Russian defense manufacturers are likely to find substantial opportunities in India's expanding defense market," through joint ventures, co-production and technology partnerships with Indian companies, Chaturvedi said.
India was the world's second-largest importer of major arms in 2021–25 with an 8.2% share of total global imports, even as its reliance on overseas suppliers dropped by 4% during the same time due to growing local design and production abilities, according to SIPRI.
New Delhi is also the world's fifth-largest military spender, with $92 billion, but this is less than 30% of Chinese military expenditure and around a 10th of America's, Wezeman of SIPRI pointed out.
India faces some practical challenges in matching China's scale of military modernization, but the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine have shown that mass-produced systems like drones can address asymmetry, Collin Koh Swee Lean, a senior fellow at Singapore's Nanyang Technological University, said.
