articles.title_orig: They bought cabins to live on a luxury cruise ship. High fuel costs got them kicked off in Cambodia.
articles.title_zh: They bought cabins to live on a luxury cruise ship. High fuel costs got them kicked off in Cambodia.
articles.content_orig:
A residential cruise ship halted operations in Cambodia on Tuesday amid soaring fuel costs , leaving passengers in limbo after the U.S. company that operates it ordered them to disembark.
Florida-based Villa Vie Residences said in a news release that it was working to identify “temporary living arrangements” for people aboard The Odyssey, a 642-foot cruise ship that launched from Belfast, Northern Ireland, three years ago and promised passengers “an unparalleled lifestyle of luxury and exploration” as it toured the planet.
Cabins on The Odyssey were for sale or rent.
According to the company , the ship can accommodate 650 residents. A Cambodian official said Wednesday there were 203 passengers and 156 ​crew members on the ship. Some passengers had already departed on ​flights, while others were waiting in the port city of Sihanoukville, Long Dimanche, deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk Province, told media.
The ship is scheduled to refuel before leaving ‌Cambodia on ⁠Saturday, he added.
An executive with the company, Mikael Petterson, declined to provide additional details in an email to NBC News. In a release this year announcing the company’s second residential cruise ship, Petterson said The Odyssey was 85% sold.
The company said in Tuesday’s release that it had taken significant measures to reduce fuel consumption but that those steps had failed to offset the spike in costs.
Global oil prices have surged since the war with Iran began this year, disrupting the world’s flow of fuel. In recent days, oil prices have climbed to their highest levels in months.
“Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution,” the company said. “Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees while we work toward restructuring and recapitalization over the next 60 days. That work is ongoing, and no outcome is assured.”
Randy Cassingham, a resident on the vessel, wrote in a blog post that he learned his journey was over after a company official posted a note on a message board for the ship shortly after 7 a.m. Monday.
The Odyssey was entering a “temporary lay up” period — indicating it would no longer be used — and everyone had to disembark by 2 p.m., the message said, according to Cassingham, who runs ResidentialCruising.com and didn’t immediately reply to an interview request.
Cassingham attributed the development to a “cascade of problems” that he would detail later.
Pamela Reckamp, who rented a cabin with her husband and disembarked this month, said in an interview that she wasn’t surprised that the ship’s journey was over.
Reckamp, 59, recalled having attended a meeting in early September at which a company official asked cabin owners to help them raise $1 million so they could leave Ha Long Bay, Vietnam.
“She said, ‘If we don’t get this money, we have about four days of the ship running,’” Reckamp recalled. “‘Then the lights will go off and the AC will go off.’”
When the ship’s financial issues were raised during another meeting a few weeks later, Reckamp recalled, a woman stood up and said she’d bought a cabin in August and hadn’t been made aware of the issues.
“I sold my house,” Reckamp recalled the woman saying. “I sold my car. I bought my home on this ship.”
Residential cruise ship halts operations over fuel costs
Reckamp said she felt terrible for the residents and the staff, who she said were lovely.
“We dodged a bullet,” she added.
Villa Vie Residences didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday night.
In a lawsuit filed last year, a company that bought a cabin on The Odyssey for $469,000 accused Villa Vie Residences of fraud, alleging it misrepresented its financial stability.
The company’s business model was not financially sound, the suit alleges, “but rather precarious.”
The plaintiffs are asking for a jury trial and unspecified damages of more than $100,000. Villa Vie Residences denied the allegations in the suit, which is ongoing.
Other cabins on the ship were available for significantly less money. Even though 85% of the ship was sold, the company said in 2024, prospective residents could still “secure their dream home starting at just $119,000.”
“When we launched Odyssey, we set out to prove that residential cruising wasn’t just possible — it was sustainable,” Petterson said in July.
Tim Stelloh is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_zh: Couple who lived on cruise ship for 2 years forced off in Cambodia after company halts operations
articles.content_orig:
Passengers on a live-aboard round-the-world cruise say they were abruptly asked to leave the ship and given only hours to disembark.
Villa Vie Residences, which operates the residential cruise ship Villa Vie Odyssey , said on Tuesday it had halted operations due to surging fuel costs.
The ship was docked at the port of Sihanoukville in Cambodia when the announcement was made, with passengers saying they were given only eight hours to disembark.
"On October 27, 2026, we received notice from the CEO at around 6 a.m. that all residents had to disembark by 2 p.m. that day," passengers Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin told Business Insider by email.
Canen and Bodin have been on the Odyssey since it first set sail in September 2024 and run a YouTube channel called Living Life on a Cruise about their experiences on board.
"We knew leaving was a possibility, but the eight-hour notice still surprised us," they said.
The couple shared a video on their YouTube channel that appears to show the moment a staff member announced that passengers must leave the ship.
"Unfortunately, they were unable to secure the fuel necessary to continue operations," a male voice says in the video.
A notice on the Villa Vie Residences website says the company is working with residents to arrange temporary living arrangements and that it is evaluating restructuring options over the next 60 days.

Mikael Petterson, executive chairman of Villa Vie Residences, told Business Insider he understood residents' feelings of shock and sadness.
"I get it. I get it. I feel awful," he said in a phone interview. "They're counting on me to make the decisions here and there's nothing else I'm focused on. I'm the villain in the story, but I'm doing everything I can to support the residents on a solution forward."
Petterson said that until last week, he was in talks with a potential investor and was expecting a new infusion of cash. When the deal fell apart, he said, the company was out of options.
Villa Vie Residences Chief Executive Kathy Villalba didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.
Villa Vie Residences said in a statement Tuesday that the surging cost of fuel since the beginning of the Iran war had made operating the cruise liner increasingly difficult.
The company said its monthly fuel expenses per cabin, which had previously averaged about $1,800, had risen as much as 344% in parts of Asia, to an estimated $6,000 to $8,000.
"Since the conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port," Villa Vie Residences said.
"Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs, and we have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses."
On August 1, Villalba, the CEO, sent residents a message titled "Urgent operational update" on an internal messaging platform. In the message, she referenced a "fuel contribution" that had been previously requested of residents. Business Insider has viewed a screenshot of the message.
"When the fuel contribution was requested several months ago, participation was not universal," she wrote in the message. "The contributions received helped some, but they covered only part of the extraordinary increase in fuel costs."
Villalba wrote that the "cash-flow" challenge had continued, and the Odyssey needed 650 metric tons of fuel, adding that fuel prices had almost doubled.
"We have now reached a critical point. The lack of full participation, combined with the unprecedented increase in fuel costs, means we must make immediate and creative operational decisions to preserve the voyage," her message said.
It continued, "We are asking every Resident who did not previously contribute to please do so now. We are also asking those who are able to provide additional support to consider helping with this immediate fuel requirement."
Villalba described the financial need as "real, immediate, and necessary to keep Odyssey moving." It went on, "This is a moment when preserving our home and continuing the voyage requires support beyond contractual minimums from those who are able to provide it."
Among the passengers asked to disembark on Tuesday with only a few hours' notice was Barbara Fiegel, 62, who has lived with her partner aboard the ship since December 2024.
"Everybody's just shocked, everybody's just saddened by this whole issue," she said. "We're still processing, trying to debate what we're going to do."
Fiegel said she and her partner booked a hotel room in Cambodia, then returned to the ship Tuesday evening and Wednesday afternoon to empty their safe and pack their belongings. "Today, as we approached, as we went back on the shuttle back to the ship, I couldn't stop crying," she said.
They plan to return on Thursday to collect their remaining items. Fiegel described the atmosphere on the Odyssey as a “ghost town.”
Joel Greiff, 57, moved aboard the ship at the start of the month and planned to live on the ship for 10 or 20 years or more. “I don’t think that will be happening,” he said.
When residents were told to disembark, Greiff emptied his cabin. “I personally grabbed everything,” he said.
He said he would like to return if Villa Vie Residences resumes operations. If not, he is planning to move to Thailand. In the meantime, he has rented an apartment in Cambodia for a month.
Greiff said he plans to return to the Odyssey on Thursday to assist other residents and “help with their luggage, help them find a place, and just start getting them and all their stuff off the ship.”
Jacob Shamsian contributed to this story.
Have you spent any time on the Villa Vie Odyssey as a cabin owner, renter, or staff member? If you have a story to share, get in touch with this reporter: jzitser@businessinsider.com .

articles.title_orig: One passport isn’t enough for some wealthy Chinese. Here’s where they’re looking next
articles.title_zh: One passport isn’t enough for some wealthy Chinese. Here’s where they’re looking next
articles.content_orig:
For some wealthy Chinese, securing a foreign passport is becoming the ultimate trade-off: giving up their Chinese citizenship.
Wealth advisors say a growing number of affluent Chinese are considering renouncing their nationality as Beijing intensifies scrutiny of offshore wealth, with concerns over taxes, geopolitical uncertainty and greater international mobility driving their interest in alternative passports.
China does not recognize dual nationality, meaning Chinese nationals seeking to acquire foreign citizenship must renounce their passports.
"We have had some clients who are willing to give up their Chinese citizenship to hold multiple passports," said Armand Arton, CEO of immigration migration consultancy Arton Capital, who added that the choice of passports depends on their lifestyle and business needs.
Meanwhile, Ryan Lin, director at Singapore-based legal firm Bayfront Law, said he has seen an increase in wealthy Chinese considering renouncing their nationality since July.
That month, Beijing introduced new measures targeting offshore trusts, with certain incomes and transactions potentially subject to a 20% tax. The changes have prompted some families to reassess how they hold and transfer assets overseas.
Previously, clients would discuss the possibility of giving up their citizenship. Now, more are expressing concrete intentions to do so, Lin told CNBC.
Manish Tibrewal, co-founder of multi-family office Farro Capital, also reported growing interest in foreign passports.
The wealth advisory firm is helping some Chinese families pursue Caribbean citizenship alongside Singapore permanent residency, with the longer-term possibility of obtaining Singapore citizenship, subject to government approval.
Tibrewal said the number of Chinese families actively exploring alternative citizenship options since July far exceeds those who have completed the process last year.
Inquiries from Chinese clients have risen 33% since July, investment migration firm Savory & Partners said, while Global Citizen Solutions reported an increase of nearly 40% compared with the same period last year.
Both firms specialize in investment migration, which helps wealthy individuals obtain foreign residency or citizenship, often through qualifying investments in their destination countries.
Renouncing Chinese citizenship does not automatically erase existing tax liabilities though.
Individuals could remain liable for taxes on historical gains, depending on how their wealth was structured, even after giving up their nationality, but a genuine change in citizenship and residency could affect future obligations, experts said.
For many wealthy Chinese, relinquishing their nationality remains a significant sacrifice, particularly for those whose businesses and fortunes are tied to the mainland.
Lin said those most willing to take that step generally have few remaining business links to China, with much of their wealth and operations already based offshore.
So where are they looking to move?
For wealthy Chinese seeking an alternative passport rather than merely overseas residency, the Caribbean has emerged as a popular choice.
Countries such as Antigua and Barbuda offer citizenship-by-investment programs that allow eligible applicants to obtain nationality through qualifying investments or contributions.
Tibrewal said Caribbean citizenship can potentially be secured within six months, making it considerably faster than pathways in Europe or the United States, where residency requirements often precede naturalization.
Arton said the appeal is less about permanently relocating and more about greater flexibility to travel and establish an international base.
Global Citizen Solutions said the Caribbean recorded the strongest growth in Chinese inquiries among the destinations it tracked this year.
European countries are also attracting interest, although many offer residency pathways rather than immediate citizenship.
"For Chinese HNWIs who are not willing to give up their citizenship, a portfolio of residencies or long-term visas is a more appealing option," Arton said.
Portugal remains popular through its golden visa program, which offers residency through qualifying investments and a potential longer-term route to citizenship.
Arton also added that Italy is attracting wealthy families through its favorable tax arrangements for qualifying new residents, international schools and financial services infrastructure.
Hungary is another emerging destination, offering long-term residency through qualifying investments starting at 250,000 euros ($290,000).
“Hungary is the one that surprises people,” according to Global Citizen Solutions. “As the larger European golden visa routes have closed or become more expensive, Hungary offers residency in the Schengen area through a regulated fund investment.”
Singapore remains attractive to wealthy Chinese because of its political stability, established wealth management industry, international schools and proximity to mainland China.
Some families are pursuing Singapore permanent residency as part of longer-term citizenship plans, although naturalization is neither automatic nor guaranteed.
Tibrewal said his firm was assisting some clients with plans involving Caribbean citizenship and Singapore residency, with Singapore citizenship a possible longer-term objective.
Australia is another popular option, particularly for families prioritizing education and quality of life.
Malaysia is also gaining attention, especially Kuala Lumpur and Penang, where lower living costs, Chinese-speaking communities and international schools appeal to families, said the migration consultancies.
"We also see interest beyond the obvious hubs in Asia, including Penang and Thailand's long-term resident visa, from families who value lifestyle and lower costs," said Global Citizen Solutions.
Meanwhile, Argentina and parts of Eastern Europe are emerging as alternative destinations for those seeking to diversify their international residency options.
Arton Capital identified Argentina as a market worth watching, while Savory & Partners highlighted growing interest in Serbia, North Macedonia and Bulgaria.
Advisors caution that interest in overseas citizenship does not necessarily translate into completed renunciations or physical relocations.
"It's important to recognize that exploring overseas residency, building a passport portfolio, and relocating an entire family are very different decisions," Arton said.

The company said its monthly fuel expenses per cabin, which had previously averaged about $1,800, had risen as much as 344% in parts of Asia, to an estimated $6,000 to $8,000.
"Since the conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port," Villa Vie Residences said.
"Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs, and we have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses."
On August 1, Villalba, the CEO, sent residents a message titled "Urgent operational update" on an internal messaging platform. In the message, she referenced a "fuel contribution" that had been previously requested of residents. Business Insider has viewed a screenshot of the message.
"When the fuel contribution was requested several months ago, participation was not universal," she wrote in the message. "The contributions received helped some, but they covered only part of the extraordinary increase in fuel costs."
Villalba wrote that the "cash-flow" challenge had continued, and the Odyssey needed 650 metric tons of fuel, adding that fuel prices had almost doubled.
"We have now reached a critical point. The lack of full participation, combined with the unprecedented increase in fuel costs, means we must make immediate and creative operational decisions to preserve the voyage," her message said.
It continued, "We are asking every Resident who did not previously contribute to please do so now. We are also asking those who are able to provide additional support to consider helping with this immediate fuel requirement."
Villalba described the financial need as "real, immediate, and necessary to keep Odyssey moving." It went on, "This is a moment when preserving our home and continuing the voyage requires support beyond contractual minimums from those who are able to provide it."
Among the passengers asked to disembark on Tuesday with only a few hours' notice was Barbara Fiegel, 62, who has lived with her partner aboard the ship since December 2024.
"Everybody's just shocked, everybody's just saddened by this whole issue," she said. "We're still processing, trying to debate what we're going to do."
Fiegel said she and her partner booked a hotel room in Cambodia, then returned to the ship Tuesday evening and Wednesday afternoon to empty their safe and pack their belongings. "Today, as we approached, as we went back on the shuttle back to the ship, I couldn't stop crying," she said.
They plan to return on Thursday to collect their remaining items. Fiegel described the atmosphere on the Odyssey as a “ghost town.”
Joel Greiff, 57, moved aboard the ship at the start of the month and planned to live on the ship for 10 or 20 years or more. “I don’t think that will be happening,” he said.
When residents were told to disembark, Greiff emptied his cabin. “I personally grabbed everything,” he said.
He said he would like to return if Villa Vie Residences resumes operations. If not, he is planning to move to Thailand. In the meantime, he has rented an apartment in Cambodia for a month.
Greiff said he plans to return to the Odyssey on Thursday to assist other residents and “help with their luggage, help them find a place, and just start getting them and all their stuff off the ship.”

Technology giant Microsoft says its profits for the three months to the end of September jumped to more than $36.6bn (£27.5bn), just days after announcing plans to cut its workforce by more than a quarter.
On Monday, the Windows developer said it would offer buyouts to around 60,000 of its workers to cut costs as it pours billions of dollars into artificial intelligence (AI).
Like many other major tech firms, Microsoft is investing heavily in the infrastructure that powers AI even as questions remain over whether such huge spending will pay off.
Microsoft shares rose by almost 2.9% in after hours trading in New York on Wednesday.
The recent financial results of tech companies have been closely watched by investors as they gauge whether the heavy spending on AI is sustainable.
Big tech companies like Amazon, Meta and Alphabet are expected to spend more than $700bn this year on AI chips and infrastructure like data centres .
Microsoft said on Wednesday that its quarterly revenue rose to $92.3bn - up 19% from a year earlier - driven by strong growth in its cloud computing business.
Its earnings were lifted by a 30% increase in revenue for Microsoft Cloud - its range of enterprise technology services.
The firm also flagged risks, including "substantial investments" in AI, among other uncertainties that could impact its finances.
The firm's chief executive Satya Nadella said AI development has helped grow the adoption of the technology and has delivered "real-world impact across every industry."
This week, the company said it would extend a voluntary redundancy offer to eligible employees in teams across Canada, India, the UK and US to adapt its workforce to "changing needs".
It will create "greater flexibility" for the firm and allow workers to leave with financial support and career planning resources, Microsoft said.
The company currently employs more than 220,000 people around the world.
Microsoft's stronger-than-expected earnings contrasted with Alphabet, as the owner of Google disappointed investors with its financial results on Wednesday.
The firm's shares fell by 9.75% after it reported a 25% drop in quarterly net profit from a year earlier and said it will continue to spend heavily on AI.

articles.title_orig: It's OK, Pokémon And Retro Gaming Fans, The Resellers And Vultures Will Eventually Move On
articles.title_zh: It's OK, Pokémon And Retro Gaming Fans, The Resellers And Vultures Will Eventually Move On
articles.content_orig:
An Inside Baseball Week dive into the sneaker market, the canary in the coalmine for these speculative vultures
If you're a fan of stuff like Pokémon cards or old video games and have been distraught at the state of things in 2026 , with resellers and middlemen wedging themselves into the market and destroying the affordability of what used to be a fun little hobby, I think there's value in considering a future where this doesn't happen anymore.
I'm not saying this as someone struck down by a debilitating and possibly terminal case of optimism. I'm saying it as someone who has seen this all before, elsewhere, and has seen how the gas eventually ran out of the speculative boom that attracted the parasites in the first place, and where things have now returned to some semblance of normality: sneakers.
I spent almost a decade, through the 2010s and into Covid, as someone who landed somewhere between "enthusiast" and "collector" on the sneakerhead scale . I've always been into shoes--I remember asking for a pair of Jordan VI Infareds for Christmas in sixth grade, and being politely told by my parents to get in the bin--but after finally growing old enough to have some disposable income, much of my 30s was spent following, talking about and buying sneakers.
Some of my favourite pairs from my collecting days
It was a lot of fun for a while there, but things started to go downhill once people from outside of sneakers caught wind of how much money was being made buying and reselling shoes. As soon as you start seeing mainstream news reports about long lines for products , limited supply, immense demand and the resulting stratospheric resale prices (as we did in the 2010s with Yeezys, Ultraboosts, NMDs and Jordan/Dunk re-releases), those products stop being 'grails' for the fans, and start becoming commodities anyone could invest in.
Nearing the end of the 2010s, manufacturers like Nike and Adidas leaned into the hype cycles created by releasing their most sought-after shoes in limited quantities. Massive online commerce platforms like StockX and GOAT grew their businesses, and what had once been an enthusiast market had been overrun by speculators and investors . A common sight on social media around this time would be photos of rooms, and sometimes even warehouses , full of sneaker boxes, as unscrupulous resellers worked out ways to engineer online auctions and retail releases to secure huge quantities of shoes that might have retailed for $150, but could be resold for over $300.
This caused enormous frustration among sneakerheads, in the same way it's causing frustration for long-time Pokémon players and retro gaming collectors now. There was literally no need for this vampiric class of middlemen to have inserted themselves between fans and their intended purchase! Manufacturers could have sold those products directly to people who actually wanted them!
Nothing lasts forever though. In 2018 the sneaker market seemed like a new frontier in consumerist money-printing, a bottomless well of demand and resale inflation, but just a few years later Yeezy had crashed and burned as a brand, Ultraboosts had run out of steam and Nike had become so reliant on milking classic silhouettes like Jordans and Dunks that it started sinking the entire company . Brands like Adidas moved away from rapper collabs and started reinvesting in performance athletic shoes, which can be bought at any store you walk into, and companies like Hoka, Salomon and On, once existing on the fringes of the sneaker market, have capitalised on a boom in running, trails and fashion trends like gorpcore to grow into major players, helping sink demand for traditional "hyped" shoes as they've ascended .
Companies like StockX remain, and there are still hyped sneaker releases, but the scene in 2026 is nothing like it was in 2016. If you want a pair of new shoes now, there's a good chance you can just jump online and get them directly from a manufacturer or specialist store. Personally I've only bought two pairs of shoes at resale since Covid: one pair on StockX at half its retail price that the seller must have accepted just to get rid of their stock, and another on Depop at retail from a guy who bought the wrong size from a running store that didn't accept returns. That's a far cry from 2016-2020, when I was camped out in Discords and subreddits, entering raffles and sharing tips on how to secure sought-after pairs.
Anyway, that brief recap is my way of not just setting the scene for the rise and fall of sneaker resale's golden age, but also to really help fans of stuff like TCGs and classic Nintendo games through their own suffering. I'm not really a sneaker journalist though, so for Inside Baseball Week I spoke with Russ Bengtson, former editor-in-chief of SLAM magazine, long-time sneaker editor at Complex and, disclaimer, author of a tome ( A History Of Basketball In 15 Sneakers ) that sits proudly on my living room bookshelf.
Luke Plunkett: Hey man, thanks for chatting with us. I've already given readers a very brief recap on the ups and downs of sneaker resale, but what do you think caused a decline in the importance of resellers in the market? Do you think it was saturation, complacency from Nike, something else, maybe all of the above?
Russ Bengtson : I think it's all of the above, and on top of that it was never something that was going to last at that level forever to begin with. You had something of a perfect storm of models—Nike in particular—from roughly 1985 to 2001, '82 if you count the Air Force 1, that were lightning in a bottle from design to marketing, that had a second life once those of us who were teens in that two-decade or so span got jobs and got money and were able to buy all the stuff we either wanted or had as kids. We had first-hand experience with and connections to all of those shoes.
As we get further away from that era, those who really wanted them are aging out and probably already have everything they wanted, and the next generation only experienced those shoes as retros. The marketing, to steal from Fight Club , becomes a copy of a copy of a copy. And then on top of that, yes, resale hubs and personal resellers already have so many pairs of all the "grail" shoes—every re-retro becomes less important—and Nike flooded the zone with so many releases that they lost their importance that way too.
LP: I guess I should be specific and accurate here: Is sneaker resale even dead? Companies like StockX keep reporting massive profits , but culturally--however you'd like to define that--it definitely seems like hyped launches and resale frenzies have dried up massively. What do you make of that discrepancy?
RB: I'm not sure it will ever be fully dead. There are obviously some shoes that still fetch absurd prices—thinking of some original '85 Jordan 1s and a lot of the more limited Dunk SBs that haven't been retroed yet. And then you have people paying resale for brands like Saucony and Brooks who weren't really in that conversation before, but now they too are doing the limited collaboration thing. And on top of that, I'm sure some people are just conditioned to buy through Stadium Goods or Flight Club or even eBay, and even on below retail sales they still get their cut. I'm not sure you're going to get as much of the "buy a whole store's allocation to drop off at a resale shop," but there will still be a resale market.
LP: Do you think, culturally at least, sneakers are in a healthier place now that the boom market has seemingly cooled?
RB: I have mixed feelings on this, and honestly on retro in general. I wrote a whole book that sought to put some of the more significant basketball sneakers into some kind of context, and what you have with retro is more or less complete context collapse. Back when retro was new and relatively rare, you had things like retro cards and even a burgeoning sneaker media trying to stay on top of things, but now it feels like it's just everything

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Two tech behemoths -- Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) -- reported earnings today. Both showed strong cloud growth, but the market is treating them very differently. Microsoft shares popped after hours while Alphabet stock sank. Why?
I think a big part of the answer is how each plans to pay for the massive outlays both have planned.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
Microsoft beat Wall Street's targets with sales up 19%, reaching $92.3 billion. GAAP -- generally accepted accounting principles -- earnings per share (EPS) came in at $4.92. Adjusted EPS was $4.89, above the roughly $4.72 the Street expected. Azure, its cloud platform, grew 48%, reaching $33.17 billion in revenue.
Alphabet's cloud growth was even stronger than Microsoft's: 103% growth for the unit, earning $11.1 billion in operating income on $30.7 billion in sales. Overall, sales jumped 25%, reaching $127.6 billion, slightly missing estimates, while GAAP EPS actually fell from $2.87 to $2.12. Search and YouTube ads also underperformed.
Some of Alphabet's EPS drop can be explained by an $8.7 billion net loss on equity securities, but even if you remove this -- worth $0.55 per share -- the earnings still came in well below what Wall Street was looking for.
While it's not a great look, I think the real issue the market is reacting to is the company's cash picture. Alphabet spent $51.4 billion on capital expenditures (capex), up from $24.0 billion a year ago. Operating cash flow -- the cash the actual business generated -- was $42.3 billion. That left free cash flow (FCF) -- the money left after paying for its capex investments -- at negative $9.1 billion. That's worse than the negative $5.9 billion the company reported last quarter.
During the quarter, Alphabet raised $28.7 billion through senior unsecured notes and $12.4 billion from selling stock. Long-term debt has grown from $46.5 billion at the end of 2025 to $125.1 billion.
Alphabet said its capex guidance for 2026 holds -- $195 billion to $205 billion -- but said it expects capex in 2027 to "increase significantly."
Microsoft, on the other hand, is still FCF positive, though like Alphabet, that figure is moving in the wrong direction. The company reported FCF of $18.63 billion, down 27% year over year, after $39.37 billion in cash capital spending. Its broader capex figure, which includes finance leases, was $45.2 billion.
CFO Amy Hood said on July's earnings call that the company expects to stay free-cash-flow positive for its current fiscal year, though capex is expected to expand. On that call, she also said demand for its cloud services was running ahead of supply.
Microsoft at this point has a much healthier cushion in its quarterly cash flow -- more room to keep spending while it waits for those investments to pay off. Alphabet is increasingly asking lenders and shareholders to help cover the bill.
Obviously, the growth is hard to argue with, but I still think the jury is out on whether this bet will pay off for both companies. Costs are climbing, and I'm concerned the math won't pencil out long term.

articles.content_orig:
Isabel Kershner Johnatan Reiss Aaron Boxerman Qasim Nauman and Leo Sands
Israel’s political leaders were bracing for weeks of negotiations over a new government, as initial results on Wednesday showed no clear winner in a tightly fought election that many have described as a make-or-break moment for the country.
By Wednesday evening in Israel, election officials had counted about 90 percent of the ballots. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s hard-line bloc of parties held a modest lead in seats over the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot, but it appears that neither coalition will win the 61 seats needed to secure a straightforward majority in the Knesset, Israel’s Parliament.
That means both leaders would need to find support from outside their coalitions to form a government. Two Arab parties were on track to win as many as 19 seats, a strong showing that potentially gives them an important role in the negotiations, even though most Jewish parties were not eager to enter an alliance with them.
Some of Mr. Netanyahu’s allies have floated the idea that he could join Mr. Eisenkot and other centrists to form a broad unity government to stay in power. For Mr. Netanyahu, who will remain a caretaker prime minister until a government is formed, that would be a comfortable scenario.
Mr. Eisenkot faces a dilemma. He has denounced Mr. Netanyahu as unfit to lead Israel, but he has also objected to partnering with Arab parties in a potential coalition. On Wednesday, Mr. Eisenkot did not explicitly mention the Arab parties but said he was focused on forming a government that was both Zionist and committed to universal military conscription, a message that rules out alliances with both Arab and ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties.
The Joint List, an alliance of Arab parties that has emerged as a potential kingmaker according to preliminary results, said it would “do everything in its power” to remove Mr. Netanyahu from office. That could signal a willingness to back Mr. Eisenkot’s bid to form an anti-Netanyahu coalition, even if its lawmakers have not been invited to join it.
The final tally of votes is not expected to be finished before Thursday evening. Lengthy negotiations are likely to follow as political parties try to assemble a governing majority. If those talks fail, the country could head to a second round of elections — a scenario that has played out before.
Here’s what else we are covering:
Vote count: The nearly 90 percent of votes counted indicate that Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition will receive about 54 seats, Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc will get roughly 49, and the Arab parties could reach as many as 19. But the numbers could still shift.
Parliamentary control: Even if no government is formed, the Israeli Parliament will open on Nov. 10, and Mr. Netanyahu’s opponents could be well-placed to take control of the legislative process. Read more ›
Herzog’s role: President Isaac Herzog of Israel holds a largely ceremonial position, except after national elections, when it falls to him to select who gets the first crack at forming a new government. Read more ›
What Israelis think: The day after Israel’s election, almost everyone in the country was asking the same question: What now? The Times spoke to people from across the political spectrum to get a sense of their hopes and fears. Read more ›
For decades, Israel’s Arab parties have been relegated to the margins of Israeli political life, often sitting on the sidelines while Jewish parties assembled a governing coalition in Parliament and picked a prime minister.
Heading into Israel’s pivotal election on Tuesday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned his supporters that the Arabs were “trying to steal the election,” though electoral officials said there were no reports of widespread irregularities. He repeatedly invoked the specter of Arab voters to galvanize his right-wing base, vowing to keep them out of power.
Mr. Netanyahu’s leading rival, Gadi Eisenkot, largely declined to answer whether he would partner with Arab parties if necessary to topple the Netanyahu government, though he said none met his conditions as potential allies.
But record turnout on Tuesday by supporters of the Arab parties looks to deliver them their largest vote totals in generations, possibly since Israel’s establishment 78 years ago.
Now, the Arab minority represents a political reality that cannot be ignored.
Turnout in the Arab community, which represents about 20 percent of Israeli citizens, appears to have translated into a stunning windfall of parliamentary seats — potentially as many as 19 combined between the two leading parties, Raam and the Joint List alliance. The Arab parties have 10 seats in the outgoing Parliament.
Israel’s future could turn in part on whether Mr. Eisenkot decides to take the political risks of partnering with them. Without their support, Mr. Eisenkot and his alliance will almost certainly fall short of the 61-seat majority required in the 120-seat Parliament to form a new government and end Mr. Netanyahu’s hold on power. Mr. Netanyahu’s alliance also looks to fall short of 61 seats.
Many Israeli Jews have long objected to building a governing coalition that relies on Arab party backing for a majority. Some say a Jewish state should be ruled exclusively by Jews. Some cite national security reasons, questioning whether Arab leaders who see themselves as part of the wider Palestinian people can be entrusted with crucial matters of state.
Those objections became even more acute after the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks on Israel and the subsequent rightward shift in Israeli politics. Both Raam and some members of the Joint List condemned the assault, although they have also been highly critical of how Israel has conducted its war against Hamas in Gaza.
The Arab parties for many years were themselves reluctant to join governments that oversaw the Israeli occupation of the West Bank and Gaza. And turnout among Arab Israelis has traditionally been lower than Jewish turnout, reflecting doubts about their ability to influence national decision-making.
Raam, a socially conservative party with roots in Islamist politics, has achieved some acceptance in Israel’s mainstream by putting less emphasis on the cause of Palestinian statehood. But the Joint List, an alliance of three smaller parties that includes a joint Jewish-Arab leftist faction and a Palestinian nationalist faction, is seen as more antagonistic toward Zionism.
Initial election results show that the Joint List will be the significantly larger of the two in Parliament.
“Netanyahu knows that without the Arab parties, there’s no majority to unseat him. That’s why he incites against us,” said Yousef Jabareen, the leader of the Joint List alliance in an interview. “The opposition should reject that incitement.”
He added: “The ball is now in Eisenkot’s court. Whoever wants to remove Netanyahu and change his policies — we are ready to cooperate to topple his government.”
Political analysts say the Joint List would be more likely to support Eisenkot from outside the governing coalition, for instance by agreeing to block any no-confidence votes. There is some precedent for this: In the 1990s, then Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin relied on Arab lawmakers to prevent the collapse of his own minority government.
Arab citizens, some of whom view themselves as both Israeli and Palestinian, experience a tension that can cut to the heart of daily life. Unlike Palestinians in the West Bank — who live under Israeli military rule — Arab Israelis can vote, and some have held high office, including on the country’s Supreme Court.
But they largely live in separate cities and towns from Jewish Israelis and retain tight familial and historical bonds with Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza. Many view themselves as second-class citizens in the Jewish state, saying they face discrimination in housing as well as neglect in receiving public services.

At least 68 people were killed and about 100 were injured after a high-speed train smashed into a stationary train in Spain on Wednesday.
Crews are now working with flood lights to search for anyone else trapped in the wreckage as investigators try to figure out what led to the tragedy.
What we know : A computer system failure led to an issue with the safety system along a 63-kilometer (40-mile) stretch of track between Madrid and Seville causing all trains in the area to be stopped automatically, said Óscar Puente, the country’s transport minister.
Puente said Adif, the state-owned company that manages Spain’s railways, then took manual command of the system and allowed the high-speed Renfe train to continue southbound toward Seville despite a red light. That train later collided with the stationary Iryo train.
Response: More than 500 emergency personnel have been deployed to the site, the Spanish Interior Ministry said. The Civil Guard said investigators are using drones to create a 3D reconstruction of the area and determine the accident’s possible causes.
Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said authorities are working hard to identify the cause of the crash and vowed that any negligence, if identified, will be addressed with “utmost firmness.” This is the third rail incident in Spain this year.
CNN’s Billy Stockwell, Michael Rios, Pau Mosquera and Duarte Mendonca, Jennifer Hansler, Sophie Tanno and Sol Amaya contributed reporting to this post.

Around 500 demonstrators gathered outside the Transport Ministry, with some throwing bottles and flares at police, Reuters reported. Video showed police deploying tear gas in an attempt disperse the large group gathered.
Protesters held signs saying “Leave!” next to a picture of Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, while others held signs saying “Criminals” and “Corruption kills.” Sanchez’s socialist PSOE party has suffered a series of setbacks and corruption scandals this year involving close associates that have tarnished its reputation.

Puente said Adif, the state-owned company that manages Spain’s railways, then took manual command of the system and a decision was made to allow the high-speed Renfe train to continue southbound toward Seville despite a red light. That train later collided with the stationary Iryo train.
CSIF, an independent trade union and civil servants’ association, accused Puente of using a “hardworking person” as a scapegoat instead of “assuming his responsibilities.” The trade union also said it had warned in September of “excess hours in Adif’s working days.”
CNN has approached Spain’s transport ministry for comment.
CNN’s Lauren Kent contributed reporting.
Renfe, Spain’s state-owned national railway operator, announced it has suspended service Thursday between Madrid and the Andalusia region.
One of Renfe’s trains was involved in a deadly collision earlier today, which killed at least 68 people. The Renfe train plowed into a stationary train operated by the private company Iryo, at a time when all train traffic in the area was disrupted due to a problem with the LZB train management safety system.
The collision occurred on the route between Madrid and Seville and an alternative transportation plan will be provided on Friday, Renfe said.
The service suspension also applies to trains coming from Barcelona and Valencia to Seville and Malaga, Renfe said in a post on X .
Some of cars derailed and officials are still searching for anyone trapped in the rubble.
Ana has been searching for her husband, Pepe, all day. But so far, no luck.
She raced to Madrid as soon as she heard about Wednesday’s deadly train collision in the Spanish province of Toledo, she told Reuters. Pepe was traveling on the high-speed Renfe train that crashed into the stationary Ilyo train while heading from Madrid to Seville.
Ana, who only provided her first name, told Reuters that Pepe’s name was not on the list of victims who have been identified.
Local police did however find Ana’s dog, who had been traveling with Pepe.
“Poor thing, I think he’s had a bad time,” she told Reuters, speaking from a school in Urda – the town closest to the site of the train crash – where relatives have been advised to wait.
Renfe, a state-owned railway company, said it had opened a special phone line for families of victims, Reuters reported.

Officials will use things like surveillance cameras and data recorders on the trains and on the signaling system to piece together how the trains were moving and how they ended up on the same piece of track.

The Federal Reserve voted Wednesday to hold its benchmark interest rate steady . "The Fed is leaning into patience. It seems they prefer to wait for more information on the appropriate level of rates, as uncertainty reigns supreme in light of recent geopolitical developments." —Phil Camporeale, chief investment strategist, JPMorgan Wealth Management.
"The Fed has time on its side ... But the direction of travel remains clear. The Fed is still taking back some of last year's rate cuts, and the two dissents underline that tightening bias. "We hesitate to characterize his communication as particularly dovish or hawkish ... The bottom line is that the Fed policy reaction is not a black-and-white, binary thing ... The market has adjusted to Warsh's communication style, but there might be a ways to go before they are fully on the same page." — Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist, Jefferies .

articles.title_orig: Election polls in New Zealand continue to show no clear outcome
articles.title_zh: Election polls in New Zealand continue to show no clear outcome
articles.content_orig:
New Zealanders will head to the polls on 7 November to elect a new government.
The rising cost of living, unemployment and healthcare are among the main concerns of voters, who will choose members of parliament.
There is no clear frontrunner, based on pre-election polls. The incumbent centre-right prime minister, Christopher Luxon, won the last election in 2023 with a promise to "build the economy".
Here is everything you need to know about New Zealand's 2026 general election.
New Zealand holds a general election every three years and uses a Mixed-Member Proportional system or MMP.
Each voter makes two choices - the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.
The candidate in a constituency with the most votes wins and becomes an MP.
Political parties on the other hand must win at least 5% of the total party votes to secure a seat in parliament. The seats are also allocated proportionately - if a party wins 40% of the total party votes, it will get 40% of the seats alloted for parties.
The New Zealand parliament typically has 120 seats - 71 are allocated to constituencies and the remaining 49 are distributed to parties proportionately.
New Zealand elections rarely result in an outright majority and parties forge coalitions to form a government.
New Zealand adopted the MMP in 1996 to address concerns that small parties were being left out of the vote.
The current government is led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, whose centre-right National party came to power in 2023 . It governs in coalition with the ACT and New Zealand First parties.
His party emphasised economic management, restoring a budget surplus, and expanding KiwiSaver, New Zealand's retirement savings scheme.
The main opposition is the centre-left Labour party, led by former prime minister Chris Hipkins.
Labour has focused on reducing living costs, improving healthcare and transport, and investing in housing, jobs and public services.
National's coalition partners also have their own priorities. ACT, led by David Seymour, has advocated stricter immigration policies, while New Zealand First, led by Winston Peters, has proposed changes to voting eligibility, with the party proposing that voting in New Zealand should be restricted to citizens only.
The Green Party, co-led by Chlöe Swarbrick and Marama Davidson, is another player. It has campaigned on issues including wealth taxes, renewable energy and public services.
Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, is also competing for parliamentary seats, with housing, healthcare, education and constitutional reform among its priorities.
Cost of living is a major concern for New Zealanders.
A September 2026 Ipsos survey found that 63% of respondents identified inflation and the cost of living as one of the country's most important issues. Healthcare and hospitals came second at 44%, followed by the economy at 34%.
Unemployment is also a growing concern, with 21% of respondents identifying it as a major issue in the same survey. It overtook housing to become New Zealand's fourth most important issue.
Polling places open from 09:00 local time on 7 November (20:00 GMT 6 November). Voting ends at 19:00. Advance voting started on 26 October while overseas voting began earlier on 21 October.
Preliminary results will be released progressively from 19:00 on election night through New Zealand's official election results website. These initial results will not be the official final count.
The Electoral Commission is scheduled to declare official results on 27 November, after the counting and verification process has been completed.
A clear result on election night could provide an early indication of which parties are best placed to form a government. However, a tight race could delay negotiations if no party wins an outright majority.
New Zealanders may therefore have to wait beyond election night to find out which parties will form the next government and who will lead the country for the next three years.

President Donald Trump’s conflict with Iran has become a political liability for his administration. Since the last U.S. strikes on Iran fell on Sept. 8, Trump has publicly ruled out attacking Iran before the November midterm elections—and promised to end the conflict after them.
Then, rumblings grew that U.S. and Israeli military planners had reportedly drawn up new strike options against Iran, including the possible use of the largest non-nuclear weapon in the American arsenal: the GBU-43/B, also dubbed “the Mother of All Bombs”.
The targets purportedly would be Iran’s nuclear facilities and energy infrastructure, though there are doubts about whether the bomb could penetrate Iran’s most deeply buried sites. According to these reports, Trump apparently is seeking a strike he could present as a military victory and then end the war without appearing to back down.
But such an approach risks triggering a far wider war than Washington intends. Tehran remains unlikely to let Washington end the conflict quickly and, fearing a potential attack from the U.S., could itself strike first. Either scenario could lead to a new round of fighting far more destructive than the last.
Reports of military plans involving “the mother of all bombs” came against the backdrop of two other worrying developments. First, Iran has been escalating its naval attacks, likely in response to increased flows through the Strait of Hormuz. Notably, two UAE-owned cargo ships, the GFS Pride and the Cape Dao , were struck in the Strait as part of this sharp uptick.
Secondly, diplomatic efforts appear to have hit a wall. In late September, Trump rejected the proposal Tehran had put forward on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly: an end to fighting on all fronts, including Lebanon; the lifting of the U.S. naval blockade and oil sanctions; the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets; and the reopening of Hormuz within seven days. Instead, Washington insists that Iran must take steps regarding its nuclear program as part of the package, something Iranian leaders say they will only do at a later stage.
The timing of any U.S.-Israeli attack remains uncertain. While Trump has said he will not resume attacks before the midterms, Israel held its election on Oct. 27, a week earlier, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had reportedly sought renewed fighting before both elections.
American and Israeli objectives may differ, of course. Trump appears to want something he can portray as a spectacular military victory without having to undergo another prolonged war, while Netanyahu’s rhetoric about “ finishing the job ” suggests more ambitious goals, potentially including toppling the Islamic Republic. Tehran seems to be preparing for either scenario with its own response: a prolonged, region-wide war designed to impose devastating economic costs.
The dominant perspective in Tehran is that the next war must be fought in a way that makes it so costly that a future U.S. president would not contemplate another. Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesperson for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), said in late September that Iran “will not stop until we have driven the United States out of the region, punished the aggressor, and established permanent deterrence so that no one will dare attack Iran.”
That logic, should it prevail, rules out a symbolic, tit-for-tat exchange. In Tehran’s view, a limited American strike on Pickaxe Mountain , the fortified nuclear site near Natanz that Trump has repeatedly evoked, followed by a limited Iranian response, would send Washington precisely the wrong message: that it can attack Iran’s nuclear facilities, register domestic political gain, and pay a limited, acceptable cost. Iranian officials have therefore warned that even a symbolic, non-lethal strike would trigger a broad response, denying Trump the quick exit he may have asked of his war planners.
Under this scenario, Iran would target regional energy and economic infrastructure. “In a region where we cannot sell oil, no one will sell oil,” Ghalibaf has warned . The UAE is particularly exposed: Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, has accused it of oil “ smuggling ” in cahoots with U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM). Rezaei also identified new potential targets: undersea cables, data centers, and AI infrastructure in the region, which he claims are worth “more than $2 trillion.” Ghalibaf subsequently extended the threat to regional governments and investors, threatening that anyone providing “funding, equity, land, or energy” to AI companies that “facilitate military aggression” against Iran “will face coercive action.”
If raising the cost of war is the first instrument in Iran’s calculus, duration is the second. Ali Balali , an adviser to the IRGC’s Aerospace Force commander, suggested Iran would conserve its arsenal in preparation for a prolonged confrontation, rather than expend it early. Two days later, Iranian Army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia argued that the enemy’s weak point is a prolonged war.
Timing is a third dimension in Iranian thinking. Iranian military officials have increasingly mentioned the possibility of striking first, preemptively. Akraminia stated that if Iran were to conclude that an attack by the U.S. and/or Israel is imminent, “we will certainly engage in preemptive warfare.” Mehdi Mohammadi , strategic affairs adviser to Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, went further, arguing that a successful strategy requires not only striking first but also delivering a decisive blow capable of “changing the balance.” There is thus at least the possibility that Iran might move early, and then fight long.
That could occur due to miscalculation resulting from ambiguous American and Israeli signals: leaked strike plans, carrier and amphibious deployments, and aircraft approaching but not entering Iranian airspace. Military experts in Iran see this pattern as an effort to normalize military activity and regain the element of surprise. Tehran could thus mistake military signaling for an imminent attack and strike preemptively, even though it may not want another round of war.
The fourth element concerns the range of those Tehran would hold responsible in the event of an attack. On Oct. 5 Ali Abdollahi , chief of staff of Iran’s armed forces, declared that if the United States acted against Iran “directly or indirectly through Israel,” Iranian forces would retaliate against the United States. The warning carries more weight in the wake of Trump’s decision to openly back Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s election. Indeed, some in Tehran interpreted this as a signal that Washington would allow Israel to strike Iran after the midterms. As a result, Tehran has made clear that even were Israel to carry out the attack on its own, U.S. forces and assets in the region would face retaliation.
This interpretation suggests that the scope of Iran’s response to a U.S. strike likely would be far wider. Its conduct in Hormuz since late September offers a preview of how it could broaden the conflict. When the UAE, backed by CENTCOM, kept oil moving through a southern corridor along the Omani coast, the IRGC shifted its attacks from small shuttle tankers to supertankers and stated that vessels using the “illegal corridor” would be “pursued and interdicted across the region.” Strikes followed off the UAE coast and near Qatar. An escalation in the region could drive Iran to go after vital energy and other infrastructure across the Gulf.
Iran’s regional partners also could widen the conflict, although Tehran does not fully control their actions. articles.title_orig: With 90% of votes counted, Netanyahu bloc has 53 seats, Eisenkot’s 48; Arab parties surge to 19
articles.title_zh: With 90% of votes counted, Netanyahu bloc has 53 seats, Eisenkot’s 48; Arab parties surge to 19
articles.content_orig:
The leader of Israel’s Balad party has condemned the country’s main political leaders for refusing to form a coalition with Arab parties, even after a record showing in polls could make them kingmakers for the next parliament after no clear winner emerged.
Sami Abu Shehadeh told Al Jazeera that Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about a fifth of the population, are being treated as illegitimate partners despite their turnout.
“This is racism,” he said. “We are a legitimate elected leadership of the national minority. The vast majority of our people decided that we are their leadership.”
Arab parties are on course to win a record 19 seats, giving them potentially decisive leverage over the main political blocs. With 85 percent of the vote counted, Israel’s Central Elections Committee has Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc ahead with at least 53 seats, and the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot on 48.
Both are short of the 61 needed to govern. Netanyahu says Israelis chose a strong right-wing government, while Eisenkot says they voted for change.
Abu Shehadeh, who leads Balad, one of the Joint List’s three parties, was not a candidate.
Israel’s elections committee voted to disqualify him at the request of far-right Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who accused him of supporting the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack due to an article issued the following day in which Abu Shehadeh called it an “important historical event”.
Abu Shehadeh subsequently told the Supreme Court he did not support “armed struggle” but acknowledged that a paragraph in the article had been incorrectly worded. He said his intention was to call for moving the conflict towards a political process.
He withdrew in October after a majority of the Supreme Court panel appeared willing to approve the disqualification. He rejects the grounds and said the court had made clear that Israel has “two different judicial systems, one for the Jews and one for the Arabs”.
“We are very proud of the Arab Palestinian minority in Israel that went in this very high percentage of voting,” he told Al Jazeera. The community’s first promise to voters, he said, was to prevent “this gang of criminals” from returning to power, naming Netanyahu and far-right ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Ben-Gvir. “So our first promise, we can keep it from now .”
Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, said Netanyahu “has scared off everybody from talking to the Palestinian Israeli parties”, leaving him best placed to “call the shots”. She said that Eisenkot and his allies have indicated that they want a Zionist government and “do not want to form a government” with the Arab parties, leaving them few options.
Danny Ayalon, a former Israeli ambassador to the United States, told Al Jazeera that turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel came in “really unprecedented numbers” and that the parties “are going to have some significant clout”.
Mathematically, he said, Eisenkot’s bloc could join forces with the two Arab parties and pass the threshold, though it would take “political wizardry”. Yousef Jabareen, who leads the Joint List, has said his alliance’s “hands are extended” to oust Netanyahu.
Abu Shehadeh set out what Palestinian citizens want from the next government.
“We are against genocide and we are against apartheid. We want to promote a different political alternative, one which is based on the values of freedom, justice and equality for both people who are living between the river and the sea.”
Of Netanyahu, he said: “Our problem … is that he is a war criminal.”
A UN commission said in a report published on Monday that Israel has continued to commit genocide in Gaza after last October’s US-brokered ceasefire in the enclave.
The Hague-based International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu in 2024 for war crimes during the Gaza war.

articles.title_zh: Microsoft earnings live: Microsoft beats Q1 expectations on top and bottom line on AI growth
articles.content_orig:
Technology giant Microsoft says its profits for the three months to the end of September jumped to more than $36.6bn (£27.5bn), just days after announcing plans to cut its workforce by more than a quarter.
On Monday, the Windows developer said it would offer buyouts to around 60,000 of its workers to cut costs as it pours billions of dollars into artificial intelligence (AI).
Like many other major tech firms, Microsoft is investing heavily in the infrastructure that powers AI even as questions remain over whether such huge spending will pay off.
Microsoft shares rose by almost 2.9% in after hours trading in New York on Wednesday.
The recent financial results of tech companies have been closely watched by investors as they gauge whether the heavy spending on AI is sustainable.
Big tech companies like Amazon, Meta and Alphabet are expected to spend more than $700bn this year on AI chips and infrastructure like data centres .
Microsoft said on Wednesday that its quarterly revenue rose to $92.3bn - up 19% from a year earlier - driven by strong growth in its cloud computing business.
Its earnings were lifted by a 30% increase in revenue for Microsoft Cloud - its range of enterprise technology services.
The firm also flagged risks, including "substantial investments" in AI, among other uncertainties that could impact its finances.
The firm's chief executive Satya Nadella said AI development has helped grow the adoption of the technology and has delivered "real-world impact across every industry."
This week, the company said it would extend a voluntary redundancy offer to eligible employees in teams across Canada, India, the UK and US to adapt its workforce to "changing needs".
It will create "greater flexibility" for the firm and allow workers to leave with financial support and career planning resources, Microsoft said.
The company currently employs more than 220,000 people around the world.
Microsoft's stronger-than-expected earnings contrasted with Alphabet, as the owner of Google disappointed investors with its financial results on Wednesday.
The firm's shares fell by 9.75% after it reported a 25% drop in quarterly net profit from a year earlier and said it will continue to spend heavily on AI.

articles.content_orig:
Qatari mediators on Sunday handed Iran a new draft deal to end the war, the Reuters news agency reported, citing an official briefed on the negotiations.
Tehran is considering the proposal and set to respond by the end of the week, the agency reported Wednesday.
The source added that there were concerns in Tehran before the meeting on Sunday that Israel could resume its bombardment of Iran this week.
The cost of the Iran war has risen to an estimated $47 billion, according to an estimate from the U.S. military's Central Command obtained by CBS News Tuesday.
Like previous estimates, it does not include damage to U.S. military bases in the Middle East. The bulk of the cost, $29 billion, is for replacing expended munitions.
According to a report released by the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office in September, the Iran war could cost approximately $2 billion to $3 billion per month for as long as it continues.
Exit polls from Israel's major television networks project that a majority of Israelis voted against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition in Tuesday's election, but his Likud party still emerged as the largest party among all the contenders. Neither bloc, Netanyahu or the opposition, has a clear majority.
While Netanyahu appears to have won fewer votes than his main challenger, according to the early exit polls, both candidates will likely struggle to cobble together a coalition.
One or the other would need to obtain majority support in Israel's 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset, in order to form a government.
Israel's two Arab parties won more seats in parliament than in any previous election. That electoral success comes after what some Arab voters told CBS News was a difficult time for them in the country under the hard-right government of Netanyahu, prompting a historic turnout for the minority community.
Both Netanyahu and those opposing him have vowed not to form a government reliant on Arab parties, arguing it would endanger the country if they gain enough seats to influence Israel's engagement in its myriad conflicts. Arab citizens of Israel are around 20% of the population.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft Reports Quarterly Cloud Sales That Beat Estimates
articles.title_zh: Microsoft Reports Quarterly Cloud Sales That Beat Estimates
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft shares rose 4% in extended trading on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results, driven by 48% growth in its Azure cloud infrastructure business.
Here's how the company fared relative to LSEG consensus:
Microsoft's revenue grew 19% year over year in the quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, according to a statement , with Azure now its biggest single business.
The software giant has been rapidly building out data center infrastructure to meet artificial intelligence demand, while also maintaining positive free cash flow unlike its fellow hyperscalers. Microsoft reported  $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, up about 30% from a year earlier. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount had projected $50.67 billion.
Microsoft flagged a higher growth rate for cash paid for property and equipment than overall capital expenditures, which include finance leases, because of "timing differences between receipt of goods and payment and a lower mix of finance leases."
Around 75% of capital expenditures are now tied to short-lived assets such as Intel chips and Nvidia graphics processing units, up from about 66% in the past three quarters and half in the year-ago quarter. The shift indicates Microsoft's prioritization of infrastructure it can can quickly turn into revenue.
Free cash flow declined 27% to $18.63 billion. Cloud rival Alphabet reported more than $9 billion in negative free cash flow in the quarter after Meta said last week its cash flow turned negative for the first time.
Microsoft's net income increased to $36.63 billion, or $4.92 per share, from $27.75 billion, or $3.72 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude a roughly $200 million loss on its investment in OpenAI.
For the first time, Microsoft disclosed revenue from its Azure cloud in dollars, at $33.17 billion in the quarter. Analysts polled by StreetAccount expected $32.32 billion. The growth rate in the June quarter was 42%.
Microsoft reported results under two operating segments — Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.  For the past 11 years, the company had three segments that divided up its Azure, Office and Windows businesses.
In Agents and Infra, revenue rose almost 25% to $76.8 billion, more than the $75.63 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. The segment contains Azure, along with Microsoft 365 cloud products, productivity and server licensing, industry solutions and frontier and support services.
Revenue in the Devices and Consumer business slipped 3% to $15.48 billion, beating the StreetAccount consensus of $15.05 billion. The unit includes search and advertising, Xbox, devices and Windows operating system licenses sold to device makers.
Sales of devices and Windows licenses declined 22%, as higher memory and storage costs elevated prices. The company pointed to the end of support for Windows 10 last year and weak PC demand.
As of Wednesday's close, Microsoft shares were up about 10% year to date, trailing the S&P 500 index, which has gained 13% over the same period.
During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft said it would cut 4,800 jobs , and followed up by announcing on Monday that it's offering buyouts to up to 60,000 employees, as it strives to balance a costly AI build-out with capital efficiency. Microsoft also established, during the quarter, an AI implementation unit and revealed a Copilot AI "super app" with coding abilities.
Executives will discuss the results with analysts and issue guidance on a conference call starting at 5:30 p.m. ET.

articles.title_zh: Fed meeting recap: Warsh says central bank will host fewer rate-setting meetings in future years
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Reserve voted Wednesday to hold its benchmark interest rate steady . At the press conference that followed, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh disclosed some of his thinking about where the U.S. economy stands, and how that affects monetary policy. But for Fed wonks, the big news may have been Warsh's disclosure of some procedural changes ahead.
Here are five key takeaways:
"The Fed is leaning into patience. It seems they prefer to wait for more information on the appropriate level of rates, as uncertainty reigns supreme in light of recent geopolitical developments." —Phil Camporeale, chief investment strategist, JPMorgan Wealth Management.
"The Fed has time on its side ... But the direction of travel remains clear. The Fed is still taking back some of last year's rate cuts, and the two dissents underline that tightening bias. We expect a hike in December and another in early 2027." — Seema Shah, chief global strategist, Principal Asset Management .
"We hesitate to characterize his communication as particularly dovish or hawkish ... The bottom line is that the Fed policy reaction is not a black-and-white, binary thing ... The market has adjusted to Warsh's communication style, but there might be a ways to go before they are fully on the same page." — Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist, Jefferies .

articles.title_orig: Trump says US will beat China in AI as technology emerges
articles.title_zh: Trump says US will beat China in AI as technology emerges
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Artificial intelligence has emerged as the critical sticking point between the U.S. and China. President Donald Trump, who has named it “super intelligence,” insists the U.S. will beat China in the AI competition.
Trump said while campaigning for president that tariffs would form the crux of the bilateral relationship. The U.S. and China, the world’s two largest economies, have been engaged in a trade war during both of Trump’s terms.
Speaking Sept. 13 in Ireland, Trump said the U.S. is leading China in AI.
“We’re leading China in AI, we’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins,” Trump said.
During a state visit to Beijing in May, Trump praised Chinese President Xi Jinping.
“And it’s to me an honor. We’ve had a fantastic relationship. We’ve gotten along. When they were difficulties, we worked it out,” Trump said.
Trump hosted Xi at the White House in September for a state visit. He touted what he called “the tremendous strides” he and Xi had already made on national security, trade and technology.
At the summit, the U.S. and China agreed to extend a trade truce until January. No agreement was reached on implementing safeguards for AI.
Trump and Xi are set to meet again in China next month.

articles.title_orig: Trump admin sues Utah to save Kalshi from the state’s total ban on gambling
articles.title_zh: Trump admin sues Utah to save Kalshi from the state’s total ban on gambling
articles.content_orig:
Firm calls charges, which include violating state gambling ban and profiting from illegal activity, ‘crazy overreach’
Utah on Wednesday filed criminal charges against prediction market operator Kalshi and two of its executives, months after a federal judge rejected Kalshi’s effort to prevent Utah from enforcing its strict anti-gambling laws against the activity.
The felony charges could represent a new tactic in how states try to assert regulatory authority over the fast-expanding activity, a clash that appears headed to a showdown at the US supreme court.
The charges include 13 counts of violating the state’s prohibition on gambling and another charge involving profiting off illegal activity.
The state’s charging documents name Kalshi and its co-founders, chief executive officer Tarek Mansour and chief operating officer Luana Lopes Lara.
In a statement, Utah attorney general Derek Brown said Kalshi has continued to operate in Utah, despite a federal court ruling that Utah’s gambling laws apply to the company.
“Gambling is illegal in Utah, whether you place the bet, run the game, or promote it. Calling it a ‘prediction market’ doesn’t change what it is, and being federally registered doesn’t put a company above the law,” Brown said in a statement.
The attorney general’s office did not immediately say what sort of criminal penalties it would seek in the case, although the felony charges carry the possibility of jail time.
In a statement, Kalshi called the charges a “crazy overreach” and said that “Utah is clearly playing politics”.
“We look forward to putting a stop to this in court, just like we did in Arizona,” it said.
Utah has been on the front lines of a battle between states and the federal government over who regulates the markets. Litigation has spread across roughly 20 states, creating a fragmented legal landscape that analysts say will likely be settled by the supreme court.
Kalshi has maintained that prediction markets fall exclusively under federal jurisdiction and are not governed by state gambling laws.
